Post.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure today to bring forward concerns I have heard over the last two years I have been in Parliament about what primarily is happening in Canada Post, concerns which people in my riding and across Canada have voiced over the difficulties they are experiencing with service within that organization.
If we consider the situation around the world, probably the most changing technology is in communication. It is my opinion that Canada Post represents in Canada a very, very important means of communication which must serve Canadians to its utmost, must smooth its process and make certain that every Canadian, whether living in the far north, metropolitan Toronto, Vancouver or the maritimes, receives a service that is first and foremost number one.
How Canada Post Corporation deals with this type of quality service which we need is going to be fundamentally important to all of us. In rural Canada its dealings with this type of service seems quite strange to me. In rural Canada corporate post offices are being closed; in rural Canada the 5,221 post offices that existed in 1986 are dwindling. Today about 1,000 of those post offices
have already been closed or converted. What has this done to rural Canada? This has taken away the only federal presence in many small communities. It has taken down the federal flag in those small communities. It has left those small communities without the pride and the privilege of Canada's presence.
This has eliminated about 3,000 jobs at the same time. Those jobs in small communities are very important. In most cases they are relatively low-paying jobs, but I think another significant point here is that 80 per cent of those jobs are for women. We are seeing women in small rural communities losing the privilege of working and helping others in those communities.
We have eliminated the one-stop service of Canada Post. In certain cases, mail is now picked up in one location and other postal services, the services one would expect to have, at counters, are being done elsewhere. In some cases, rural Canadians have to travel as much as 12 miles in order to receive service today which they could have counted on just a few short years ago.
What have we heard the government say on this issue? The government and Canada Post Corporation maintain that changes in postal service, for example a closure or a conversion, would only take place under certain circumstances. Canada Post and the government have suggested these circumstances would only be through resignation, retirement or promotion of a postmaster, loss of a postal site, or local initiative. In other words, they have very clearly set out the premise for which closures would occur. These are called by the government "natural occurrences". The correspondence that I have been receiving suggests that natural occurrences are not the means by which many Canada Post facilities are being shut down.
A small community, Mossley, Ontario, stated in a letter to me just a short while ago: "Canada Post Corporation has promised and continues to advertise that communities of Canada are given a 90-day period of meaningful consultation before community consent". A period of consultation was never offered to the Mossley

May 31, 1991

community. The Mossley post office will be shut down on June 28, 1991.
It is interesting to note that I have a letter from the member for London-Middlesex who represents Mossley: "By working together, as Minister Andre said himself on Mossley Heritage Day, June 6, 1987, we can ensure that the Moseley post office remains operational for at least another 122 years". It is being closed this June. What a change in position.
I also have the notes from the statement of the minister at that same meeting. He very clearly stated that Mossley post office was secure, adding that he hoped it would remain that way for another 122 years.
The minister, speaking to a group of heritage people in Mossley in 1987 suggested that this government would protect our post office and make sure it remains open. Now, five years later, there is a total change of commitment.
It appears that the guidelines, the rules and the regulations that have been set forth for rural closures are changing day by day, month by month and week by week, but not to improve service to Canadians. Let's be very clear. The primary goal of Canada Post service to Canadians is the goal that is being tom apart by the actions of this government. However, a very unnatural occurrence happens every time a Canada Post office gets closed in these communities.
Across Canada, 157 post offices have been targeted for closure or conversion in a very short time. Across Canada, another 250 jobs will be lost. I would like to point out that I have a listing of post offices that are scheduled to be closed. I can say very clearly that there is a full sheet of the names of post offices to be closed in Ontario. Post offices are to be closed in maritime Canada; Newfoundland, Labrador, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and in Quebec. There are 63 closures scheduled for Ontario, 18 for Manitoba, 22 for Saskatchewan, five for Alberta and seven for British Columbia. Every province in this country will have several closures.
This list, by the way, comes from negotiations with Canada Post, and it is a Canada Post target list.
The hit list.

A very good point.
We realize that we are talking about 150 communities which are going to lose their postal outlets the way they see them existing today.
Across Canada, another Canadian institution will be dismantled. In front of every post office, the presence and the pride of all Canadians flies. We know that when people see our flag in our communities, it brings pride and respect to them, to their community and to their families. When we see the elimination of post offices, we also see the elimination of the symbol "Canada" in these small communities. That is what is happening. That is what this government is permitting Canada Post Corporation to do.
The government will argue that natural occurrences give rise to Canada Post action, that in each of the 157 cases a natural occurrence has happened. Did it? Or did Canada Post utilize a January 1991 agreement with the Postmasters Association to push nature along, an agreement which stated that over an interim period of time it would eliminate part-time workers?
Where a Postmaster had retired or was urged out of the job by certain offerings of Canada Post, the post office became available to be shut down. I think there are very many actions taken in Canada Post to unnaturally close post offices. In some post offices, term employees have been doing the work of regular employees for over two, three, four years and longer.
The work has been getting done. The people have been working for Canada Post, but now those people are done.
What criteria does Canada Post use to decide on post offices to be saved or post offices to be sacrificed? In 1991, in Quebec, Canada Post has targeted 12 post office conversions to date. Yet, Canada Post Corporation has advertised to staff 12 group-type post offices and seven grade-type post offices.
The group-type post offices are very small. Hopefully, Canada Post will staff these and will not let the competitions expire without filling the positions.
Why do 12 small post offices close and 12 group and 7 grade post offices have post office job competitions? What are the criteria? Where is the quality of service? Where is the equality of service for 7 communities in
May 31, 1991

Newfoundland and Labrador, 15 in Nova Scotia, 4 in Prince Edward Island, 2 in New Brunswick, 12 in Quebec, 63 in Ontario, 18 in Manitoba, 24 in Saskatchewan, 5 in Alberta and 7 in British Columbia?
Equality will end this summer as we see Canada Post's massive campaign to convert the 1991 crop of post offices into oblivion. It is not only through Canada Post Office conversions that the government and Canada Post attacked rural Canada. Earlier this year, rural Canadians dodged another bullet fired by the government with, as a result of the government's policy direction, the elimination of a postal subsidy program. Canada Post was preparing to pass increases along to community weekly newspapers, which would have increased mailing costs from 200 per cent to 1,000 per cent.
How does that affect the lot of our average Canadians? Letters have come in to my office, and I thought, Madam Speaker, I would relate to you one which came from my home community. This was sent in to the Kingsville Reporter, in my home town, by a person who was very distressed at the fact that these postal rate increases would alter her ability to have the newspaper delivered.
"I was just ready to seal my envelope with a cheque for the Reporter covering the period to June 1, when-cancellation-cancellation when I read your editorial. I do not feel we can pay all that extra money to a government I absolutely abhor. It has brought nothing but depression and disillusionment into my life. Now that we are both retired and watching our pennies a little more carefully, I cannot, in conscience, let Jack send off the subscription cheque for such an increased amount."
Now we are going to hear from the government that it has put a delay on those rate subsidy changes. However, it has only put a delay on rate subsidy changes in postal code 2. Postal codes 3 and 4 already have those subsidies decreased. They are going on presently and it appears that by March those increases will go ahead.
I have talked to people from many, many, many small newspapers across this country and it has been very, very clear. Loss of subscription, loss of revenue, loss of news and loss of communication is the result of this govem-
Supply
ment's callous way of looking at subsidies in rural Canada.
We have seen losses in transportation: VIA Rail and Air Canada. We have seen losses in CBC. We have seen losses with Canadian small newspapers. I wonder: would the same actions be taken against Canada's daily newspapers if in the same situation? Would this government stand against the great dailies in this country? I do not believe so. I believe the actions are usually taken against the small who are unable as a unit to protect themselves as well.
The postal rate subsidy given to rural Canada was given for a very specific reason. I would like to take a second to quote Bill Pratt, President of Canadian Community Newspapers Association. In his article he states:
I mean, dammit, I thought we had a pretty good relationship going for the past couple of centuries. There was even a time when politicians thought newspapers were important. The thoughtful knew newspapers could be a valuable tool for bringing people together through sharing of information.
Some politicians encouraged establishment of papers, and, because papers were a vital part of the political and social infrastructure, they decided to subsidize delivery of those papers to readers through the postal service.
The relationship began to cool a few years back. I'm not sure why, but I suspect it was about the time they invented "Canada Post".
I like to think we might discover some intelligent life form in Ottawa: that someone will realize community newspapers can mean a lot of business for Canada Post at very little real cost;
I think he is putting on the line a very direct comment: communication in small, rural Canada, communication in distant regions is just as important as communication in major cities. The government should be concerned about those people in outreach areas who need a little help because of the vast size of this country and because the local communication in smaller towns is not as efficient as The Globe and Mail. They also cannot have advertising and other costs that one might get from a major newspaper.
Coming from a community like Windsor, seeing a small newspaper close is going to be very drastic to that community. We saw CBC close; we saw the end of local news on television. Are we to see the end of local news in the media, in the local newspaper now? It appears we

May 31, 1991
Supply
are heading in that direction under this government and Canada Post's policy.
Early this year, rural Canadians did dodge that bullet, but I would suggest to this government at this point in time that it make eveiy effort to re-analyse postal subsidies and not just say it is going to put a moratorium on it for nine months; re-analyse it and look at a fair system for all Canadians across this country.
I believe it is extremely important that rural Canada gets its fair share.
What I would like to do is go back to a statement that was made when this newspaper legislation came in. The newspaper legislation did come in on the basis that the government House leader, in response to a question I had in the House, said that rate increases would only be 25 per cent. On further inspection, rate increases for rural newspapers came up as high as 1,000 per cent. I think the decision was made on a very ill-timed, very ill-conceived bit of knowledge that the government had. It has certainly hampered rural Canada tremendously.
Finally I would like to come to the point of the government's idea that it has become a much more lean, efficient organization for Canadians. We have heard the government brag about the profits that Canada Post has shown. The government, for its part, did not listen to all Canadians on concerns, but it certainly was very proud that in the last year, 1988-89, it showed a profit of $96 million and that in 1989-90 it showed $149 million.
May I just point out that in those two years it also received $500 million in subsidy from the Canadian government. That certainly throws a different angle on what it is bragging about. The profits of Canada Post have only been gained through a $500 million subsidy.

Madam Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague for his very thorough analysis of the problems which are facing Canada Post at this time.
He mentioned the problems in his area of southwestern Ontario. I too come from a highly populated area in
the Niagara Peninsula. He mentioned some assurances that he received from Canada Post at an earlier time.
My question to him concerns the fact that assurances were given to him directly, and to the people in his area, about keeping the post offices open, and he used the term I believe, "at this time". I too have received that kind of assurance from Canada Post. I was told that the post offices in Welland, Thorold, St. Catharines and Niagara Falls will be kept open, notwithstanding the fact that Canada Post has put in a huge sorting plant in Stoney Creek.
I would like his opinion as to how much credence I should put into these assurances that the post offices for which I am responsible in the Niagara Peninsula would not probably suffer the same fate as many of his have suffered.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank very much my colleague for that very good question. It does bring into perspective an issue that I happened to see yesterday here in this House: statement one, statement two. It appears that from time to time, and I am not sure how long a time period, everything changes. The example of Mossley in my opinion well illustrates a situation where a minister said: "This post office will remain open for another 122 years. No questions. No worries. No problems". However, just a few short years later the post office is scheduled for closure.
There are 157, and I have got the listings of each one of those post office here in this document which came from the negotiations with the union and Canada Post- it is Canada Post's documentation-closures listed on this document.
We know that what is said at one time, over a long period of time, could change. It seems that there have been statements made politically which change very rapidly. I have a major concern that we do not have solid policies suggesting where we are going. We see changes occurring. That type of thing happened, I believe, with the postal rate increase.
The opposition on this side of the House and the back bench on that side of the House shook enough fences that there was a delay in the increase. It was very political.
May 31, 1991

This government must examine its policies, clarify its policies and tell the Canadian public where we are going-not piecemeal, and chop, chop, chop Canada Post apart.

Madam Speaker, I too want to compliment my colleague from Essex-Kent for an excellent presentation on his valid conclusions as to what is happening with Canada Post in this country, and where we as a nation should be going.
He mentions several regional areas in the country that are being hurt and also the people in this country who are being hurt. For many years the rural post office was what bound communities together, it was the meeting place where people gathered.
With our current great concern with national unity, this should be a major consideration of this government when it considers closing rural post offices.
My question has an economic basis. If we examine the position of Canada Post during the past two years, we will find it is true that on the books Canada Post shows profits of $96 million in 1988-89 and $149 million in 1989-90. This is what Canada Post shows as a profit. Yet for the same two years almost $500 million was paid to Canada Post as subsidies to offset certain mailing costs. That eliminates that so-called profit that Canada Post is claiming.
For almost two years the 46,000 CUPW workers have been without a contract. Since July 1989, 46,000 CTC employees have not received wage increases. While Canada Post boasts of profits, it conveniently takes almost $500 million in subsidies and does not give its work force a raise.
What would happen if these points were factored into the statements of Canada Post Corporation? I am sure there would be no so-called profits, and the numbers would be inclined to prove it.

I thank my colleague for a very astute question, one that illustrates our consternation. Many times in this Parliament partial truths are told, the whole picture never being revealed.
The government has been telling us for two years that Canada Post is in the black, that Canada Post is a
Supply
profit-making corporation with profits of approximately $100 million two years ago and $150 million last year.
That is total fiction. The truth is that we support the Canadian government in its endeavour to subsidize Canada Post, don't get us wrong on that. However, the truth has to be told that there is a $500 million subsidy to Canada Post for regions, for disabled people. Those subsidies must remain for communication.
The other point made by my colleague is that two years of negotiations have not brought a contract with Canada Post employees yet it states that it has a profit of $100 million, $150 million. Once it settles that negotiation there will be retroactive pay which has not been taken into account anywhere in the documents of Canada Post, meaning that the $100 million and $150 million-and we are talking about 60,000 employees-may not all be there. It may be another sham.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to the members of this House about the services offered by the Canada Post Corporation.

Canada Post is organized in 10 divisions with a head office located in Ottawa. Canada Post has a national customer base of about 26 million people and over 1 million businesses served by more than 16,700 locations where postal products and services are available.
With approximately 47,000 full and part-time employees Canada Post also deals with more than 7,800 entrepreneurs across the country who provide mail transport and delivery in urban, suburban and rural areas. Canada Post delivers, on average, 40 million pieces of mail every working day, serves over 11 million addresses in every part of Canada, walks, drives and flies over some of the most formidable terrain in the world in some of the worst weather conditions. It runs a network of 26 major mechanized processing plants, buys more transportation services in Canada than any other corporation, and Canada Post makes a profit.

May 31, 1991
Supply
When Canada Post became a Crown corporation, its revenues were in the $1.5 billion range and yet it had no modem standards, systems or procedures and no balance sheet or general ledger in place.
The management team had to put these into place to improve and expand service and break even financially while business was proceeding full speed ahead.
In its bleakest year, Canada Post cost taxpayers around $600 million. That was more than nine years ago. Since then the corporation has moved from that deficit to a profit of $96 million in the fiscal year 1988-89, which was the first in over 30 years, and to $149 million profit in the fiscal year 1989-90. That profit allows Canada Post Corporation to invest in new equipment which will improve postal services.
The biggest story, which you do not see in the headlines, is that at the same time Canada Post has improved the reliability of and accessibility to its services, increases in the basic letter rate have been limited to less than the rate of inflation. In real terms, the price of a stamp has actually decreased. Canada Post is committed to giving Canadians more reliable, accessible and affordable service.
Let me explain what the people at Canada Post have been doing to improve postal service in each of these areas. With respect to reliability, Canada Post has set up a program of operational improvements for collecting, processing and delivering mail. Uniform standard systems and procedures were introduced at all processing plants so that mail would move in a co-ordinated, predictable way across the country.
For example, a special system for colour coding the mail has been instituted. This allows employees to designate which mail should be treated with priority within a postal facility in order to maintain service standards.

The corporation's National Control Centre is linked to nine divisional control centres, and its role is to monitor mail flow 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Corporation management meets every morning at the control centre to evaluate the results of the past 24 hours and measure them against projections. This procedure is essential,
Madam Speaker, because in this way, Canada Post can evaluate its performance in terms of meeting its commitments and take specific action to make it even more competitive on the market.

This state of the art technology has won the corporation international acclaim. Canada Post is vigorously marketing the management system on the international scene with success in New Zealand and the United States.
One may recall news articles announcing a multi-million dollar contract with the United States Postal Service and Systemhouse, based on technology used by Canada Post. Clearly defined standards for the delivery of properly prepared letter mail were established, and an independent firm of auditors, Ernst and Young, was hired to measure Canada Post's performance regarding those standards and publish the results every quarter.
Canada Post is one of the first postal administrations in the world to have its performance independently measured and the results published. Other postal administrations such as USPS have implemented a similar procedure and the results show that they have a long way to go to achieve similar results to Canada Post.
The delivery time standard here in Canada for properly prepared letter mail is within two business days within the same urban centre, within three business days between major urban centres in the same province, and within four business days between major urban centres in different provinces.

In fact, Madam Speaker, the results have confirmed Canada Post's progress. For instance, Canada Post is the first postal administration in the world, as I said earlier, to have its performance measured by an independent auditor and to have these findings made public.
The last report by the firm of Ernst & Young for the quarter ending in March 1991 shows that, at the national level, 97 per cent of local mail was delivered in accordance with the standards to which Canada Post is committed. These performance standards were met, Madam Speaker, while setting a priority on outstanding customer-oriented service. Three factors are involved in providing this service and maintaining this priority:
May 31, 1991

reliability, accessibility and reasonable cost of products offered.
To achieve this, Madam Speaker, the Canada Post Corporation embarked on an operations enhancement program for mail pick-up, processing and delivery. It has put in place the requisite standards, systems and procedures in all its facilities, to ensure that the mail is routed across the country in a manner that is co-ordinated, controlled and predictable.

The people at Canada Post are constantly looking for ways to improve service performance to those set standards. By using resources more efficiently, better service to customers can be provided and costs for providing the service can be managed more responsibly.
Another indication of reliability is the greater volume of mail delivered. That volume has increased by 38 per cent since 1981. By trusting Canada Post to deliver more of their mail, people are showing confidence in its ability to provide efficient and reliable service.
Canada Post promised to make its products and services more accessible. The corporation's goal is to make it easier for customers to buy stamps, mail letters and receive packages. That is why Canada Post is extending its century-old traditional partnerships with local businesses and setting up retail postal outlets with the people who best understand retail sales: the small businessman or, as I should say, the small business person.
This program will increase the number of outlets by more than 25 per cent over the next five years. This is only the beginning. Canada Post has one of the most extensive delivery networks in the world, serving over 11 million addresses throughout the country. Over each of the next five years, an estimated 225,000 new addresses will be added to this network.
One of the biggest demographic changes in Canada over the past 20 years or so has been the growth of sprawling suburbs around our major cities and towns. The community mailbox is one method used here as well as in the United States to extend service to suburban areas. One of the advantages of community mailboxes is that they have special compartments for packages.
Supply
At the present time, the corporation has approximately 27,400 community mailbox sites across the country serving approximately 712,000 customers. Under the Community Mailbox Implementation Program, a further
6,000	sites are scheduled to be opened in the fiscal year 1991-92, which will serve about 157,000 additional customers.
Retail postal outlets located in communities across Canada offer extended hours, giving customers greater access to products and services Monday to Friday and on the weekends.
Canada Post business is increasingly meeting its competition, not only private courier companies, but the avalanche of electronic message transmission technologies. In order to stay in business, it must provide its customers with products and services which meet their needs. Canada Post is doing just that. A system for letters and parcels which allows both customers and commercial customers to choose the best speed/cost combination for their needs has now been introduced through various parcel products.
Canada Post wants to regain a significant part of the parcel delivery market. It is making parcel products more competitive and attractive to commercial customers, providing both regular and expedited services.
In meeting the challenge of the electronic age, Canada Post offers customers electronic mail, Telepost, Intel-post, Envoy Post and volume electronic mail, which usually provide next day delivery. For an added cost, Telepost and Intelpost can provide same-day delivery for top priority messages. Priority Courier will deliver urgent documents the next morning, guaranteed. Canada Post provides timely information on delivery status and location via the track and trace system. Special letter products offer unfeatured courier service which also guarantees delivery within the purchased time frame as early as the next day, or the customer receives a new special letter envelope of equal or greater value, free.
The corporation has also made significant inroads in the commercial market with its own unique advertising medium called Ad Mail. Using the postal code in combination with demographic and socio-economic data allows Canada Post to compile a variety of data on any targeted market. Adding this to the extensive network and flexibility makes it possible for mailers to distribute

May 31, 1991
Supply
advertising material in areas as small as one carrier route or as large as an entire region, to all the rural communities in a given area or to all of Canada.
Another commitment to Canadians is affordability. When Canada Post became a corporation nearly nine years ago, Canadians were promised they would get their money's worth. Since then, basic letter rate increases have been kept below the rate of inflation. Comparisons are often made between postal rates in Canada and other countries without taking into account the different wage rates, geographic sizes and population densities involved.
Canada is the second-largest country in the world and our relatively small population is widely dispersed. By comparison, all of Great Britain would fit into an area the size of the maritimes. The basic letter rate when measured in terms of the minutes of labour required for the average worker to earn the price of a stamp is lower than in many countries. In comparison to the major OCE countries, Canada ranks second only to the U.S. In Canada, mail is moved from St. John's, Newfoundland to Vancouver, B.C. for the same price as between Ottawa and Hull.
By any yardstick, that is value for money. Canada Post is delivering on its promise of better service to its customers.
In 1989-90, as was indicated earlier, the profit was $149 million. While this amount may appear large in absolute terms, on revenues of $3.6 billion it is small. It represents a return on equity of 10.5 per cent and is a step toward the industry norms of 14 to 15 per cent. The corporation has made its second consecutive profit and for the first time has paid dividends of $60 million to its shareholder, the Government of Canada. That means that Canadian taxpayers are no longer subsidizing postal operations. They now only pay once for their postage stamp.
To Canadian businesses, which provide approximately 80 per cent of the postal volume, the availability of reliable, accessible and affordable postal service is essential. Inefficiencies in the postal network mean higher costs for businesses, increasing their vulnerability in the highly competitive marketplace.
To build the postal service for the future, Canada Post must maintain its profitability. The corporation must maintain its profitability and invest those profits into
revitalizing its aging plants and equipment, while continuing the improvement in efficiency. It must continue to increase volume by providing services which meet market needs and focus even more on serving its customers well.
Through the 1990s and into the 21st century, Canada Post will continue to improve upon its success by providing Canadians with reliable, accessible and affordable products and services specifically adapted to the needs of the Canadian consumer.
It is clear that the opposition, through its statements, would have the government direct Canada Post to move itself backward to those dark days when it was a main drain on the Canadian taxpayer.
We had good service.

I do not have much more to say. I will finish soon and you will have your chance to address whatever issue you want to address.
The responsibility of Canada Post is to collect and move the mail efficiently while at the same time maintaining self-sufficiency. It has done it. It is doing it and it will continue to do it.

Madam Speaker, in listening to the hon. minister's speech, I could not help but think about how hard the Canada Post public relations people must have been working last night to prepare.
That was an incredible statement of statistics supporting the national objectives of the corporation. Not once in the minister's speech did I hear him talk about the needs of the Canadian people.
He talks about the market needs, but whose market are we talking about? Are we talking about the market needs of Canwood, Marcelin, Gallivan and Edam, which are communities in my constituency? The market needs of those communities are directly related to the service component of Canada Post.
I did not hear one word from this government or from this minister about commitment to the policy of serving the needs of rural Canadians.
My question to the minister in the short period of time I have is twofold: First, is there a commitment from this government to needs of rural Canada? Second, when I listened to his speech, he talked about colour coding and
May 31, 1991

the way in which colour coding speeds the process of mail delivery. Is the minister aware that in colour coding blue is for Monday, yellow is for Tuesday and red is for Wednesday? If a red box arrives on Monday, it sits in the goldam post office until Wednesday until it goes out.
That mail is not being processed to service the needs of that community. It is being serviced to meet the needs of Canada Post. I would like to know if the minister is aware of that and if he is prepared to do anything to correct it.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

Madam Speaker, in his introductory remarks, my hon. colleague said that he could not help but listen to the speech. I suppose that is flattering and I thank him for listening, even if he could not help it.
On the other hand, I think perhaps that my hon. colleague, when he eventually gets the "blues", will re-read the speech very carefully and perhaps reassess his statement in general.
It is always odd to hear the opposition members of this House bitch about statistics when they are not in their favour.
Whenever a statistic comes up, regardless of the subject, if it happens to be damaging to the government they quote them every hour of the day.
In this case we have statistics which demonstrate that not only does the service improve but that the customers are happy with the service, including those in the rural areas.
Why should we not use those statistics? We cannot expect the opposition to acknowledge or even underline en passant that the majority of Canadians are happy with the improvements brought about by Canada Post which are directly for customers in general, including those individual customers in rural areas and not just the commercial customers as my hon. friend tries to demonstrate.
A little bit of clarity and honesty in statements in this House with respect to what the Government of Canada is doing for Canadians would be appreciated once in a while.

Madam Speaker, strawberry growers in Nova Scotia have recently been advised that the application of federal sizing standards will be enforced more rigorously than in previous years. The variance standard will require strawberries to meet standards within one-eighth of an inch in diameter. This precise measurement would prevent our growers from being competitive and will result in much of the crop being left in the fields and many part-time jobs being lost.
In March, the horticultural council passed a resolution increasing the allowed variance to one-quarter of an inch and although it has been approved in principle, the department has advised that the change will not be implemented in time for this year's crop.
I ask the Minister of Agriculture to address this situation and ensure that any unnecessary obstacles are removed and that this change be implemented as soon as possible.

Madam Speaker, this week marked the first anniversary of the democratic election in Myanmar, formerly Burma, during which the National League for Democracy won a landslide victory. Yet these newly elected government members are not allowed to take their seats in Parliament. The transfer of power seems no closer today than it did a year ago.
By April of this year, the military junta has arrested almost 80 of 457 elected NLD members. There are over 500 party officials now in detention. Reports of torture abound, and at least three parliamentarians have died while in prison.

May 31, 1991
I call upon the Government of Canada to demand the following on behalf of all fair-minded Canadians: First, the immediate transfer of power to the democratically elected government of Myanmar, the immediate release from prison of all members of the National League for Democracy, and that Canada officially recognize the duly elected government of Myanmar.
The Government of Canada must then bring all its influence to bear at the United Nations so that the rest of the world can also begin to do what is right for the people of Myanmar.

Madam Speaker, it is interesting and significant to note that in 1979 the task force on Canadian unity, commonly known as the Pepin-Robarts commission, said that our Frenchspeaking minorities will make more headway as a result of social consensus and provincial legislation than they will from constitutional guarantees.
That commission went on to recommend that each provincial legislature should have the right to determine the official language or languages for that province. Some are now suggesting that this 1979 task force was ahead of its time.
If, as the Prime Minister says, this House of Commons is the real constituent assembly, should we not dust off the Pepin-Robarts report and openly debate its pros and cons?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the mayor of the city of Hamilton has written me a letter advising me that at the City Council meeting of May 14, 1991, a resolution was passed condemning: "the actions of three local Conservative MPs in refusing to meet with the Finance Administration Committee to discuss the composition of the Hamilton Harbour Commission".
Shame, shame.

As most members will know, Canadians have the right to demand that members of Parliament must be accountable, not only to their constituents, but also to their communities and institutions. When a
member fails to even meet with officials of their own city, town or region, there develops a lack of trust and confidence.

Madam Speaker, documents filed before the Quebec Superior Court indicate the insidious, pernicious and unethical tactics used by tobacco industry advertisers to sell death to youth and other targeted consumers.
A 1988 advertising plan notes that very young starter smokers choose Export A because it provides them with an instant badge of masculinity, appeals to their rebellious nature, and establishes their position among their peers.
Similarly, we know young women of child-bearing age are manipulated into smoking by advertising which associates smoking with slimness, attractive appearance and popularity. Today, I rise to protest the bizarre and inhumane treatment of two particular Syrian Jews, Selim Swed and his brother Elie.
They have been imprisoned without charge for three and a half years. They were beaten and tortured during this period and were ultimately brought before a tribunal last week.

Jean Corbeil, Minister of Transport, is speaking at a ceremony where the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health is presenting Air Canada with an award for its leadership in helping to create a tobacco-free Canada. Members may be aware that today is World No-Tobacco Day.
On January 1, 1990 the Non-Smokers Health Act came into force. On that day, all inter-city buses became totally smoke-free at the owner's request. Smoking on trains was reduced to one-third of every third car and terminals and stations were limited to one-third of the area accessible to the general public.

For longer flights, a progressive reduction in the number of seats reserved for smoking passengers is still in effect. This is all part and parcel of the projections in the budget. We are taking steps to ensure that we can bring interest rates down if we deal with the inflationary pressures, the inflationary expectations. There are signs
May 31, 1991

we are making some progress and we stand by our projections that there will be growth emerging in the second half. That has all been outlined in the budget.
I ask the hon. member to reread it and particularly pay attention to page 4.

The Minister of National Revenue yesterday made a remarkable confession, a death-bed confession for this government, when he said and I quote:
We have moved too far in the taxation area, and we're in the
process of reviewing the whole thing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all I will do is tiy to respond to the hon. member with some facts which are very simple. The United States and Japan extract about 30 per cent of their Gross Domestic Product in the form of taxes. Canada extracts about 34 per cent; the U.K. and Germany, 37 per cent; France, 42 per cent; and Sweden, 55 per cent-that one country that is held up as a model by the members of the New Democratic Party.
I realize that that may not provide solid comfort, but the fact of the matter is that until we deal with the fundamentals, as the former Minister of Finance indicated, the key to growth and prosperity is to bring down interest rates, and the way to bring down interest rates is to remove the inflationary pressures and deal with the deficit problems throughout the country, and indeed all the provinces have to join in that effort. That is what is going to bring about sustainable growth. That is what will bring about price stability and that is the tack we are on. I am convinced it is the correct tack in this matter.

A supplementary, Madam Speaker, for the Minister for International Trade. If the government wants to make some fundamental changes and to reverse policies that are costing Canadian jobs, we better take a look at the trade deal because we know how many jobs that cost Canadians.
We understand that on June 10 the government will begin talks with Mexico and the United States here in Canada on an action plan around the trade deal. The U.S. Congress spent months discussing the trade deal with Mexico. It had a long debate, as did the Senate. It was an opportunity for the American population to hear some of the views on this, while this government has not allowed this opportunity for Canadians in this House.
Given the serious consequences of the Canada-U.S. trade deal, would the Minister for International Trade postpone his talks and put into action a plan that will include a full debate in this House on both the effects of the Canada-U.S. trade deal and the projected effects by this government of the Mexican trade deal? Workers out there know what the effects will be, and they want to hear answers.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today and speak on this motion, a motion presented on an opposition day in reply to the motion of supply.
The motion on the table today reads very simply:
That this House call upon the government to institute policies that
would require that service to Canadians be a priority of Canada
Post.
I have been the post office critic for the federal New Democratic Party for quite some time. Earlier this year I sadly turned it over to the member for Churchill, who is now serving as the federal New Democrat Party's post office critic. I am now serving in environmental areas, areas I am also very concerned about.
On behalf of the member for Churchill and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I want to say a few words about Canada Post, the service coming from Canada Post and the motion before us today.
I believe this is a very appropriate motion with very appropriate timing. It is a time when Canada Post is actively engaged in closing rural post offices. Canada Post has been acting over time in the way it deals with post offices; it started to close post offices in 1986 and just prior to the federal election in 1988, it slowed down; and then stopped closing post offices.
Shortly after the election in 1988, after the people had returned members of the government to their seats, post offices began to close again. Now we are seeing an escalation during the summer, the summer before what should be a year prior to a federal election.
In 1986, Canada Post came out with a plan which indicated that all rural post offices in Canada would eventually be closed, probably by the year 1996. Here we are engaged in a furtherance of that plan. We are seeing that the plan Canada Post talked about in 1986 is coming to fruition.
One of the hon. members just a few moments ago talked about the myth of commitments to rural Canada. We know that since 1986, 1,028 rural post offices have been closed or privatized and out of those 3,000 full or part-time jobs have been lost. Three thousand full or part-time jobs have been ripped out of the heart of rural Canada, jobs which have served those communities very well and which quite often have provided income for people who were engaged in helping with the church, the school and the business community in many forms other than just simply selling stamps to members of that community.
The motion is very appropriate because these closings are continuing. This year they have been stepped up. In
May 31, 1991

Canada this year, I believe, there are close to 250 post offices under attack and scheduled for closure, 24 of which are in my own province and four in my own riding.
I have just returned from Saskatchewan where I have already met with Canada Post in the communities of Canwood and Marsden. Next week, during which Parliament is sitting, Canada Post will be visiting the community of Edam to tell it that its post office will be closed. I mentioned that there were four in my riding. The other community is Gallivan, Saskatchewan. Its meeting with Canada Post has also concluded.
Canada Post's closing of these post offices in the three month period-the announcements were made at the end of March-of April, May and June has been greater than it has been for any equivalent period of time since 1986, when the Prime Minister and the cabinet approved the policy of Canada Post which allows for the closings to take place.
I want to quote briefly from Cynthia Patterson who is Rural Dignity's national co-ordinator. Cynthia Patterson has been working diligently on behalf of rural Canadians for many years. In my mind, she is doing a very admirable job.
Rural Dignity and Cynthia Patterson have to be congratulated for the work they have been doing.
Cynthia Patterson says: "Rural Canada's back is up against the wall with Canada Post at this time. We cannot afford to lose our post offices. The federal policy attacks the rural infrastructure, rural service and rural jobs. The Prime Minister promised in 1984 to support small towns with big dreams, but what he has done is make us small towns with big nightmares."
Very appropriate. As I said, I have just returned from my constituency where these community meetings proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that the members of those communities are experiencing the nightmare of having their post office taken from their midst.
The mandate of Canada Post is indeed one of service. That this motion addresses service is most appropriate. When the Canada Post Corporation was created, the mandate that Parliament gave to Canada Post was very simple and very clear.

I want to just state for the record, one more time, so the government understands the mandate and what the Canada Post Act says about the mandate. Section 5(2) of the Canada Post Act reads:
(2) While maintaining basic customary postal service, the
Corporation, in carrying out its objects, shall have regard to
(a)	the desirability of improving and extending its products and services in the light of the developments in the field of communications;
(b)	the need to conduct its operations on a self-sustaining financial basis while providing a standard of service that will meet the needs of the people of Canada and that is similar with respect to communities of the same size;
(c)	The need to conduct its operations in such manner as will best provide for the security of the mail;
(d)	the desirability of utilizing the human resources of the Corporation in a manner that will both attain the objects of the Corporation and ensure the leave as is commitment and dedication of its employees to the attainment of these objects; and
(e)	the need to maintain a corporate identity program approved by the Governor in Council that reflects the role of the Corporation as an institution of the Government of Canada.
Every single one of those clauses indicates the desire of Parliament in 1981 to ensure that Canada Post was delivering a service to the people of Canada, doing it in such a way that its employees felt a part of that needed service to the Canadian population, and ensured that the corporation knew that it was meeting the needs of the people of Canada and not the needs of its corporate structure.
What has happened since 1981 when this act was passed by Parliament is that a government changed. We have now a corporation that is attempting to meet the financial needs of the corporation rather than the needs of the people it is serving.
I am very committed to the needs of all Canadians and particularly to the needs of rural Canadians when it comes to getting the postal service they deserve.
One point in that regard-I want to make it very clear-is that I want the people of Canada, those who are reading the Hansard of today's debate and those who are watching on their television screens today, to rest assured that when this government changes so will this policy against Canada Post services.
No longer will rural or small communities have to pay the price of this corporation's profits. Rest assured that when this government changes, so will this polity. I am

May 31. 1991

committed to that from now through until this party forms the government and has to adopt the policies that we know will work in rural Canada.
When the Corporation Act was established in 1981, the second thing in the mandate was self-sustainability. The first element of the mandate was service, but the second was self-sustainability. We on this side of the House agreed that self-sustainability was a goal that we should be working toward within Canada Post and we proposed many different ways of dealing with it, ways in which the government and the corporation could utilize the creative ability to increase revenues and not decrease expenses, which could only come at the expense of service and the people of Canada.
The government has ignored all requests and flexibility within the network to help increase the revenues for Canada Post except when it comes at the expense of employees, people of rural Canada and the services that are provided to the Canadian population.
We must know Canada Post went beyond self-sustainability and has run into the realm of profits: two years ago, $96 million; last year, $143 million; and well on its way to its goal of a $250 million profit this year, about 60 per cent of which is supposed to be earmarked to return to the federal government. We have gone from the point whereby the users of Canada Post were being subsidized by the taxpayer to a point where the taxpayer is now subsidizing the government through Canada Post.
The corporation has taken self-sustainability to new limits and it is astounding to hear members opposite stand over there and talk about how good all of this is for Canada in general. We might note that the way in which Canada Post describes self-sufficiency is that there must be a 14 per cent return on its investment. Canada Post will not feel that it is self-sufficient until it has a 14 per cent return.
In my mind, in a government agency self-sufficiency means you do not cost the taxpayer any money and you do not take any money from the taxpayer for other purposes. Self-sustainability is a very simple concept: you simply break even on operations. Canada Post is quite able to become self-sufficient without closing a single post office in Canada.
A couple of years ago the government recognized that the Canadian population was quite concerned about the operations of Canada Post, and in trying to meet the
needs of the Canadian population it set up a committee, something called the Postal Services Review Committee. It staffed the committee and provided it with about $1 million in funds to travel around the country and listen to the concerns of people and to report back on what was happening within Canada Post. The report in November 1989 was particularly interesting. I will quote from the recommendations to the Canada Post Corporation from the Postal Services Review Committee and I think it will enlighten all members of this House, particularly government members on this issue: "The committee is deeply concerned that these changes," talking about rural post office closures, "which have reduced the level of service for some rural residences continue to be implemented. Canada Post has acknowledged that the savings to date from all 319 rural conversions," and it is almost three times that number now, "have not been material. "The corporation could, therefore, readily modify its planned activities without adverse impact on its goal of self-sustainability." In other words, according to the Postal Services Review Committee, Canada Post could become self-sustaining without the closure of one rural post office in Canada.
The report's conclusion is that: "The corporation's commitment to the objective of financial self-sufficiency and what appears to have been the corporation's concentration on improved service to large volume mailers has and continues to cause service reductions primarily affecting households and small businesses. There is room for eliminating service inequities and for improving service without putting undue strain on the corporation's financial requirements."
The group of people that this government hired to look at Canada Post operations says that this can be done without closing rural post offices and, more importantly, that what is being done is cutting services to the people who rely on the post office.
How did the government respond to this report which was tabled in the House of Commons and debated here both on the floor of the House and in committee? The government fired the committee and refused to give them any more funds to continue the work of investigating Canada Post operations. By firing the committee, it put back the entire evaluation of Canada Post operations on to the corporation itself.
May 31, 1991

Now we see the corporation hiring public relations firms and polling organizations to give us statistics which tell us that Canadians are happy with the service.
The government's own committee found out that Canadians are not happy with the service. We, who come from rural Canada, know that the people are not happy with the service that is being provided by Canada Post in any of this conversion closing or privatization policy and practice that is taking place out there.
In the meantime, what is Canada Post doing while it is closing operations and putting 3,000 rural Canadians out of work? We find out that Canada Post has just spent money to ensure that Canada Post Corporation has a box at Skydome so it can entertain its business clients while watching the Blue Jays play baseball.
The minister responsible for Canada Post in this House on May 24, just a couple of days ago, supported Canada Post's decision to buy a box at Skydome by saying that from time to time the corporation has to entertain its business clients. In the meantime, I have got a postmaster who has put in 14 years of service, has never been declared a full-time postmaster, has served her community for the last three years, and is being put out of work so that Canada Post's corporate management can entertain business clients at a ball game in Toronto. It is just a shocking indication of how much time, money and thought the government spends on the large corporate structure in this country while ignoring the needs, wishes and will of the ordinary Canadian people, the people who live in, enjoy living in and want the quality of life provided by rural communities. It is something that I am not going to forget for a long time.
I also want to indicate one thing in terms of service that I alluded to earlier in a question to the minister who was responding so well for the public relations department of Canada Post. When the minister talked about the corporation providing new service qualities for mail delivery, he talked about the colour coding delivery requirements so that you can put priority on mail. Even in my own community, a small community, the boxes arrive at Canada Post from sorting depots in some other part of Canada marked with a red tag for Monday, a yellow tag for Tuesday, a green tag for Wednesday. Purple tagged mail is not supposed to be delivered until Wednesday so the letter carriers are told: "Don't touch that box of mail, leave it until Wednesday", even though he has only got half a bag to deliver, a half-empty bag. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on this motion, moved by my colleague from Essex-Kent, that this House call upon the government to institute policies that would require that service to Canadians be the priority for Canada Post.
We are at a point now where Canadians are wondering just how far this government will permit Canada Post Corporation to go before it steps in, if at all, to restore full national postal service for the people. We have been witnessing the disintegration of postal service throughout the country. Rural and urban residents are realizing that the Canada Post of the future will not reflect its past motto of service to the people. Instead, it has taken up a bottom line corporate mentality. This policy has been particularly hard on rural communities across Canada.
Over the last month I have been involved with the people of Avonmore, which is in my riding, who have been fighting to keep their post office open. Canada Post has indicated on June 27 that Avonmore will join the hundreds of other rural communities across Canada without a post office. In fact Canada Post has made no secret of its plans to eliminate over 5,200 post offices in rural Canada by 1996.
In many cases this means that the only federal presence in these communities will be removed; the Canadian coat of arms will be taken off the wall, the flag pulled down and the building sold. At a time when Canadians are wondering about the future of Canada, it is truly amazing that the government is content to sit back and allow Canada Post to close up shop in rural Canada. What is particularly unacceptable is that the people living in these communities do not have any say in the matter. They cannot veto a decision by the corporation to close a post office. In April 1987, the second report of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations recommended to the government that: "No closure of a post office or change in postal service be undertaken without meaningful consultation and the consent of the commu-

May 31, 1991

nity affected". Obviously the government and Canada Post did not think much of this recommendation.
In the case of Avonmore, Canada Post sent a letter to the residents informing them in no uncertain terms that a traditional post office would not be maintained in Avonmore after June 27. It invited the people to attend a meeting with Canada Post and the community to discuss total service for Avonmore after the closure.
At this meeting the people were bluntly informed that their post office was going and there was nothing they could do to reverse the decision. The so-called 90-day consultation period with the community is a joke. How can you have reasonable consultation if one party is told what is going to happen and you must accept it? This is not constructive dialogue. This is dictatorship. The people of Avonmore left their meeting angry, upset, and naturally resolved to fight this closure every step of the way.
I have received numerous letters from the people of Avonmore on their meeting with Canada Post. Each one clearly outlines the disgust felt at the manner in which Canada Post conducted the meeting and their frustration and helplessness over the lack of participation in the decision to close their post office.
One of my constituents in Avonmore wrote me asking how in the world did these people get so much power. She went on to say: "I can appeal the decision of a judge. I can appeal the decision of Revenue Canada taxation, but Canada Post can tell me that is just how it is as they devastate my small community and I cannot appeal the decision taken by people who clearly know nothing at all about rural communities".
The people of Avonmore are steadfast in their resolve to save their post office because after it closes there will be no retail postal outlet to provide postal services to the community. There will be no conversion in Avonmore, just straightforward elimination. There is only a limited number of businesses in the community and no one wants to operate an RPO.
As a result, Canada Post has indicated that it will install mailboxes somewhere in Avonmore. However, to buy a stamp or register a letter, residents will have to
travel 24 kilometres to the nearest available post office. Imagine, 24 kilometres to obtain such a basic service as purchasing a stamp.
This is outrageous in a country such as ours. There are a lot of elderly citizens in Avonmore. How are they going to get to the post office in Finch? What happens if they do not have transportation?
Is postal service in Canada going to be available to only those with a car? This is incredible. Rural Canadians are being made second-class citizens by a second-class Canada Post. We should be getting a rebate from Canada Post. It is not improving to meet the challenges of the next century, it is going back to the pony express and the people of rural Canada better own the pony.
Canada Post has promised to provide equal or better service to any community which loses its post office and where an RPO is established. However, the corporation is strangely silent about its promise when an RPO cannot be provided. Canada Post, like the government it represents, likes to brag about how successful and popular its RPOs are. It simply chooses to ignore the many cases across rural Canada where residents have no mail service beyond a mailbox by the side of the road.
In the Postal Services Review Committee's recommendations to Canada Post, in November 1989, the committee stated that some of the corporation's customers have been undeniably disadvantaged by the rural conversion program. The committee stated, and I quote: "There are households in small rural communities where a post office closure has resulted in a requirement for local residents to travel to a neighbourhood community, as much as 58 kilometres distant, in order to obtain counter service".
According to the committee, at the time some 66 communities representing 3,500 households were affected by this form of reduction in postal services.
The committee went on to state that this decline in service was in contravention of Canada Post's commitment to its rural customers. The committee stated that the corporation initiated the rural conversion program, in its own words to, and I quote: "increase in the most cost effective manner access by customers to services". In contrast to this declaration, postal services in 66 rural communities were dramatically reduced. This is not good enough.
May 31, 1991

The damage being inflicted on rural Canadians by Canada Post has not abated since 1989. Right now the residents of Mabou, Nova Scotia, are fighting alongside Avonmore and other communities to keep their post office open, thereby maintaining at the same time the single most important federal symbol in their community-
Mabou is located in the constituency of my colleague for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso. The hon. member cannot be here today for this debate, but I know of his strong commitment to the efforts of his constituents in Mabou who are trying to save their post office.
Last Thursday, the people of Mabou expressed their solidarity with the people of Avonmore who had come to the steps of the House of Commons to protest the impending closure of their post office. It is rather ironic that the callous actions of Canada Post to close both of these post offices has forged a common bond between people in rural Nova Scotia and people hundreds of miles away in rural Ontario.
This is the unity Canada needs now. I am only sorry for the circumstances in which this friendship and common cause has been created. Why then has Canada Post refused to keep these post offices open?
One can only conclude that it is afraid it would set a precedent and the whole master plan of rural conversion would be ruined. If this were to occur, it would be difficult for the government to sell Canada Post to private interests. Like Air Canada and Petro-Canada, the government is trying to mould Canada Post into top financial health so it can sell it.
The government does not care about people. It does not care about rural Canada and it does not care about how it implements the master plan, as long as it is successful. Canada Post and the government should review its policy on the future of the corporation and its privatization.
I believe most Canadians would firmly support the comments made by Professors Brian Osborne and Robert Pike in the December 1990 issue of Policy Options. They adequately summarized the serious problem the privatization of Canada Post would create for Canada and our postal system. The professors stated, and I quote: "to delegate postal services to private sector actors-without any central control and direction-is to

pose a major threat to the underpinnings of social and regional integration which are, after all, the foundation of a modern nation state".
To many rural Canadians, it will always be the quality of mail service they receive which will be the most primary concern. An RPO will not provide the mail with the priority that a post office does. The argument that RPOs are opened longer than post offices and, therefore, people are receiving better service just does not satisfy rural residents.
They are, however, concerned about the security of their mail. They are concerned about the dismissal of acting postmasters and postmistresses and the part-time staff of a post office and the lost jobs in rural regions that are already economically depressed. As well, the symbolic loss of a post office reinforces the alienation rural residents feel for a cold and distant federal government, a government which is ignoring rural Canada.
Finally, what of those 66 communities which had their postal services clearly downgraded when their post offices were closed, as a result of not being able or willing to provide an RPO. Canada Post is punishing them by still going ahead and closing their post offices. The traditional post offices in all these communities should be restored.
Even the postal review committee said that such a move would "not impinge negatively on the corporation's goal of financial self-sufficiency."
The people of Cornwall are also concerned about the fate of their own post office. The main post office is located in a building that requires considerable repairs. Rather than allocate the funds to fix it up, the Department of Public Works has declared the building surplus. As it appears Canada Post will have to vacate the building, a number of my constituents believe that the corporation will use this occasion to close down this post office. To do this would have a serious negative impact on the city of Cornwall and it will also eliminate several jobs.
Cornwall wants its post office and the postal employees want to stay at work in their own community.
I trust the minister responsible for Canada Post, the corporation and Public Works Canada will endeavour to provide a similar postal facility to that currently in Cornwall located in the downtown area.

May 31, 1991

Canada Post and the government have embarked on a carefully staged selling scheme which glosses over the flaws in the rural conversion program. The corporation and the minister responsible for Canada Post never miss an opportunity to sing the praises of RPOs and how its surveys show a 90 per cent approval rating from customers who have an RPO established in their community. I doubt the value of these surveys.
Canada Post refuses to divulge the questions on the surveys. In addition, how can we give credibility to surveys which ask postal customers questions when the customers are actually in or near the RPO? Not very many people in rural Canada will bad mouth their neighbourhood storekeeper, whom they have known for years, in front of a Canada Post pollster.
One thing I can definitely say about the results of these surveys is that the 90 per cent approval figure would be somewhat lower, I might add drastically lower, if the survey was conducted in Mabou or Avonmore.
I urge the government to take the initiative and put a stop to the rural conversion program and re-evaluate the direction it has set for Canada Post. The corporation does not need to be sold off and the people of Avon-more, Mabou and all of rural Canada do not want to be sold out.
In conclusion, I join with my colleagues in the Liberal Party in calling upon the government to support our motion that the government institute policies requiring that service to Canadians be the priority for Canada Post.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member from Calgary Northeast for his comment and question.
I think it just reminds us, once again, that the government is not listening to the people. Whether it is in rural or urban Canada, Canada Post is delivering a second-class service and making citizens second-class citizens. In communities like Mabou and Avonmore, we are not talking about a conversion, we are talking about the total elimination of a post office.
In urban centres such as Calgary, and other large centres across the country, some housing developments have door-to-door delivery, others have supermailboxes. There is just no consistency. There is no equity of service across the country.

Last week we had the visit of 60 residents of Avon-more who presented me with over 700 names on petitions on a day they designated as "Avonmore's Drive for Dignity."
I hope the government, through the corporation, will re-evaluate its position.

Mr. Speaker, I want to share with my colleague from Stormont-Dundas something that is very particular to my riding, a city riding in Scarborough.
The post office in my riding did a study and it wanted to take away something like 15 boxes. It did not notify the residents of the area. All of a sudden, one morning, those boxes vanished. These were boxes from in front of seniors' buildings, boxes from areas where the seniors cannot walk more than two blocks to deposit their mail. You know, Mr. Speaker-because I know you are reaching that golden age-it is very important for grandparents to communicate with their children and grandchildren.
