Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today on this motion.
Canada Post has come a long way since the days of the traditional post office. It has had to adapt to new methods of providing services in order to respond to the evolving needs of its customers. In other words, Canada Post has had to change, as Canada has changed, and the members opposite refuse to recognize that.
In order to meet these changing needs and expectations, Canada Post has worked hard to improve the reliability and accessibility of postal services in Canada, particularly as they have related to rural customers in rural areas. In fact, there are 4,000 more outlets today than there were when Canada Post became a corporation. Four thousand more outlets out there to serve Canadians.
It has had to manage the operations of its services in the most cost-effective way and the services must be managed effectively. At the same time, the corporation has the responsibility of eliminating postal deficits that have burdened the Canadian taxpayer in the past.
As you know, 10 years ago, all three federal parties agreed with the legislation to change government policy and make Canada Post into a postal corporation. There were a number of reasons for this.
Canada Post had been faced with a great number of debilitating strikes that had resulted in Canadians being denied postal services for periods of over 40 days, and there were many of these strikes.
The reputation for service and reliability had gone out the window. It had been lost. A department that had once achieved surpluses on a regular basis, was reaching annual deficits of more than $600 million. Some of these

May 31, 1991
Supply
were threatening to reach $1 billion. A $1 billion deficit. Outrageous.
There was a new management team put in place and it began to operate the Canada Post Corporation on a model of efficiency and service to Canadians. It improved reliability, accessibility and affordability. Canada Post has met all of these services.
Uniform standards, systems and procedures were introduced to ensure that Canada Post operated as a fully integrated distribution system. It delivers an average of 34 million pieces of mail every day to almost 11 million addresses coast to coast. That is an enormous amount of mail it moves to a great number of addresses in a very short time.
It has established a national control centre which is linked by computer to airlines and trucking companies that carry the mail. It is also linked to the plants that process the mail.
This centre monitors the movement of mail 24 hours a day, seven days a week, so that situations that threaten the delivery of mail can be dealt with immediately. Because of this, the reliability of Canada Post has been much improved.
Canada Post also measures its performance. Ernst and Young sends 50,000 pieces of properly addressed mail through the system four times a year and publishes the results.
Today these reports show that Canada Post's on-time delivery performance is almost 97 per cent, compared with an average of below 85 per cent when monitoring began in the fall of 1987. In fact, other countries and other postal systems have emulated this model which Canada Post put in place.
Canada Post is working to make it more convenient for people to buy their products and access their services, whether they live in cities or in rural Canada. With the largest retail network in Canada, larger than all the banks and all the financial institutions together, in order to meet the needs of Canadians, they are making it even larger.
However, Canada Post must do this in a cost-effective manner in order to achieve the objective of affordability. If costs are high, then these costs are passed on to post office customers.
Canada Post is readjusting its retail network in urban Canada to ensure that customers have access to postal products and services at times and locations which reflect the changing shopping patterns of the majority of Canadians.
I would like to give you an example of what has happened in my own constituency of Edmonton-Strath-cona. Two years ago, a person named Mr. Eugene Baravash took over the Maurice Pharmacy which housed the McKemon postal outlet in my constituency.
Canada Post soon approached him and said: "We would like to turn your post office from a post office outlet into a franchise." Mr. Baravash said: "I cannot do it now. I do not have the money to come up to buy a franchise. I would have to expand the space requirements in my pharmacy and I will not be able to do it."
Canada Post at that time was a little heavy handed. It threatened to close down and take out the postal outlet to put it somewhere else.
I intervened with the post office and I asked the post office to give him a bit of time, to wait a year or two until his cash flow became positive. He had just taken over this store. He had heavy debts and so on.
Canada Post sat down with him and came to an agreement that in a couple of years time they would review this.
Canada Post has now reviewed it and I understand that the Maurice Pharmacy which houses the McKernon postal outlet is on its way to becoming a full-fledged franchise. What this will mean is greater service, greater numbers of hours, and a greater number of services in the post office.
Canada Post, in order to meet its goals, has been sometimes a bit heavy handed in all members' eyes. Over all, Canadians are experiencing greater service, and this is very important.
One thing we have to realize is that, according to inflation, the price of postage stamps is a better deal today than it was before. I would like to give an example

and compare basic letter rates of the major OECD countries.
To contrast the cost of a stamp with how long it takes to earn that stamp in minutes of labour: In the United States it takes 1.6 minutes of labour to buy a postage stamp; in Canada, it takes 1.68; in Sweden, 2.02 minutes of labour and so on down to France where it takes 3.09 minutes of labour to buy one postage stamp for an ordinary first class letter. In Italy it is 3.61 cents.
Canada is ahead of Sweden, Australia, the United Kingdom, Japan, West Germany, France and Italy.
Not only that, according to surveys of Canada Post many people are very satisfied with the service. On conversions that occurred between the years 1987 and 1989, there was a 91 per cent over-all satisfaction rate. Of course there has been an adjustment, and sometimes adjustment and change are uncomfortable, but once they have been made Canadians are generally satisfied.
I must commend Canada Post. There are glitches, yes, and there are complaints from time to time, as hon. members have mentioned. However, Canada Post is willing to work with members of Parliament. It is willing to work with Canadians. It is turning a profit now, two years in a row. It is taking this profit and reinvesting it into capital equipment, which is badly needed, and into mechanization. This is good for Canada Post, good for Canadians and good for Canada.
I would just like to close with one other statistic, which is that Canada Post has 97 per cent on-time delivery,
4,000	more outlets and, again, 90 per cent satisfaction. I believe that is very good.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the remarks of the member. I noticed that he of course quoted many statistics and I do not necessarily disagree with some or all of them.
However, I heard another speaker today talk about one of the decisions of Canada Post. I listened very carefully when he talked about the problem that his constituent had and the apparently heavy-handed approach that Canada Post had for this poor gentleman who was struggling in a business, like many people in Canada are struggling in business.
Supply
However, we heard another member raise the fact that this same corporation which is heavy-handed-and we all know of instances where it has been heavy-handed- apparently purchased-and I stand to be corrected, beg to be corrected, if I am wrong-a box at the Skydome in Toronto. Those things do not come cheaply.
Does the member know anything about the following? If it is a fact that Canada Post Corporation purchased a box at the Skydome, allegedly for the purpose of entertaining their clients, first of all, does he agree with it? Second, has his constituent been invited by Canada Post to attend a ball game in its skybox?

Yes, I believe Canada Post did get involved in renting a skybox. That was raised in the House last week. At least 80 per cent of the mail, and it could be 85 per cent of the mail, delivered by Canada Post is business mail. There is a large volume of business users. Canada Post is like any other corporation that needs to keep good relations with businesses which provide it with the bulk of its mail and the bulk of its revenue. A large amount of this revenue which is obtained from business users is used to offset some of the services it provides to Canadians. I think that is important.
The corporation is involved in several major Canadian sporting and entertainment facilities, including the Toronto Skydome. It purchases tickets to sporting events in other parts of the country, not unlike businesses.
The member also mentioned heavy-handed. The corporation tries as best as it can to negotiate with Canadians and with businesses, and I applaud it for that. Sometimes for their own interests business, outlets or people are resistant to change. Canada Post at some point in time has to make a decision. We all realize that. It is just like in the House of Commons: we debate and we debate and debate, but the day comes when we have to make a decision. Canada Post is not inflexible. It will change its decisions. At the end of the day it must make a decision and it must move forward.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this debate. I welcome the opportunity to do so in response to the opposition day.

May 31, 1991

I guess some of the mistakes of Canada Post in the past are legend. There is no question that before it was made a Crown corporation by this government, the corporation was running into all kinds of difficulty. In fact when we took office in 1984, we made a commitment to the Canadian people that we were going to take the $500 million deficit and turn it around. Him it around we did. We have taken that $500 million deficit and turned it into a $150 million profit. I do give the minister of the day responsible for Canada Post some credit for doing that.
The down side of that, and there is always a down side to any cost-cutting measure, is that rural Canada has paid the price for that turnaround. It is almost the story of the city mouse versus the countiy mouse. If you listen to all of the debate on Canada Post in this House, you will notice that most of the criticism of Canada Post is coming from rural members of Parliament like myself who have numerous communities within their rural ridings. That is where the heart of the problem lies with regard to Canada Post.
I want to give some examples. They are not exaggerations but facts. Drivers who drive their own vehicles to deliver mail to rural parts of my riding and many other ridings in this country are getting paid at a rate far less than the mail delivery service in cities. Where a letter carrier service is provided by Canada Post, the letter carriers have a contract, a fairly strong union, and are actually paid more to deliver mail in town without the cost of an automobile than these poor drivers in rural Canada. This is an example of the absurdity of situations within Canada Post.
Drivers in my riding have delivered the mail for years. In fact I was speaking to one of them yesterday. They have decided they are not going to go after the contract, in other words put a bid in or retain the contract to deliver mail in their particular area, because they can no longer afford to do it. It is as simple as that. They are working for less than minimum wage. It comes down to the absurdity within Canada Post of two different situations, two different unions, no union, one working for less than minimum wage, the other working at a far higher wage with fewer expenses.
It is the same with rural post offices. We have had numerous post office closings and conversions in my riding. Rural post offices were in themselves not totally responsible for that $500 million that we inherited when we took office and took over Canada Post. Far from it. The postmistress or the postmaster in those post offices in many cases is working for slightly above minimum wage. Compare their wage scales with the wage scales in the city post offices. There is a vast difference.
That is why members of Parliament on both sides of this House, like myself, get very irritated when they hear of the closing of some of these rural post offices. Granted, sometimes it makes sense and I am sure we can document that. If I have time I will document cases where conversions have worked. In many cases it does not work and it is not working. That is another example of some of the policies that Canada Post forced on the people with no discussion, no dialogue at all. They simply arbitrarily did it.
The best example I have of that is the mode of delivery. Each Canadian is entitled to one free mode of delivery in this country.
In rural areas it usually means a rural mailbox. If I have a rural mailbox, I am entitled to free delivery. For some reason, and it usually comes down to age and a problem of inaccessibility for a rural Canadian to actually walk to the end of the driveway-sometimes driveways in rural Canada are 200 feet long, 300 feet long and sometimes longer, sometimes shorter-but some Canadians, because of a handicap or whatever, cannot get to their mailboxes. They choose, instead of getting mail in a mailbox, to pick it up in town or have a relative pick it up.
Do you know what Canada Post did, Mr. Speaker? The rental of a box in a post office went from $26.50 to $50 in one year. Many residents phoned me about that, wondering why their rental fee went from $26.50 to $50 in one year. I could not explain it.
Name one corporation in this country that can raise prices by 100 per cent and get away with it, where the consumer would actually allow them to get away with it. I do not know of any. Canada Post did, as the member on the other side is nodding, and did get away with it.
May 31, 1991

Those are the types of things that just turn rural Canadians off when we are speaking of Canada Post. It is very negative. Canada Post has no thought at all for rural Canadians.
There is a little community in my riding called Fredericton Junction. This one is the most absurd case of all. There was a surplus of lock boxes in this particular post office in Fredericton Junction. Canada Post arbitrarily decided that anyone farther than .4 kilometres from this particular post office would be forced to erect a mailbox. In other words, they would be getting rural delivery once they were beyond the bounds of that post office by .4 kilometres, just a little less than half a kilometre. Many of the residents in that community are elderly. Many of them obviously are not. They are still working Canadians like you and I. They preferred to walk down to the post office and get their mail. Canada Post arbitrarily threw this decision at them. They are outside that .4 magic number that Canada Post invented. What they are forced to do now, if they want mail in that little post office, is pay the $50 to walk down to get their mail which yesterday was free. Absurd. To top it off, in this particular post office, most of the residents could not, even if they wanted to, erect a mailbox.
Some of the points I have raised have been taken care of by Canada Post, by just getting in there and fighting tooth and nail to make sure that some of these minor changes take place. Why does Canada Post not start listening?
Members of Parliament have just about zero clout when it comes to Canada Post, as everyone here will nod their head to just about zero, a big fat zero.
Some members.

All members. The parliamentary secretary to the minister responsible for Canada Post might have some clout but the little country mouse in rural Canada does not have any clout with Canada Post, none at all. If you can embarrass it publicly, sometimes Canada Post will respond to complaints by members of Parliament. That is the only tool that I have, to stand up on my hind legs in this place and complain.
It is always the urban members of Parliament who get up and defend Canada Post, because no one from rural Canada in their right mind can get up in this House and

defend it. Monday through Friday, there is not one who could get up on his or her hind legs in this House and defend Canada Post. Its decisions are mostly arbitrary. Canada Post has actually lied to members of Parliament.
This morning a senior member of Parliament told me of a situation in his town where a staff person at Canada Post simply fell asleep at the switch, did not inform his office as to what was going on and then attempted to cover up. That is a recurring theme with Canada Post. It is one that I do not want to see continued.
That is why I will stand up on my hind legs in this House any day of the week and defend my rural Canadians.

I have listened to a number of speakers who have been focusing on the plight of people in rural Canada as it relates to the post office and I wholeheartedly agree with them.
I want to say that the situations are no different in the metropolitan areas. I would like the member to comment on a couple of things that have been happening in the metropolitan areas.
For example, in my riding of Surrey North, there has been a privatization of post offices, particularly in the drugstores. We have had an incident where the comer drugstore had been running the post office for a number of years and a new owner came in. There were nine women working there, earning between $7 and $8 an hour doing the postal work. He immediately informed them that they were taking a reduction in pay, losing their seniority and that he was cutting back their hours. They finally formed a union and went on strike.
The post office assisted that employer every way it could to bust the union. It brought mail in. It kept the post office going, which was simply being ran by the employer as a loss-leader. The community was disrupted. The people who had served that community well were out of work. Finally, the whole drugstore, because it was owned by a big chain and did not want to allow adequate wages in one store because it might have to have it in another store, shut it down. That is being repeated over and over in this whole thrust of privatization.

I would like the member to comment. I appreciate the difficulty in the rural, but what about us in the metropolitan areas?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot comment as effectively and as passionately on urban areas because I am not a member of an urban area and do not represent an urban area, but I know they are not without their difficulties.
I would like to point out something, although it is not directly answering the question: One of the things Canada Post does very effectively with regard to public relations is send out information notices to the communities. It does it through the community's member of Parliament as if the member could change it. Canada Post offers to meet with the mayor or the council in the cities and villages concerned and explain the process as to how the mode of delivery will be changed. Taking the post office out of that community would be a more accurate way of stating it.
It encourages the community to get involved. It will send out a questionnaire, which is a totally loaded questionnaire because it only gives three options. I mention this for a particular reason and I hope I have time to explain thoroughly.
Canada Post will give three options: a green box, rural delivery or a retail outlet. In most cases, if the communities had a choice it would be number four; maintain the service they presently have. That one certainly is not mentioned. The third one, the retail outlet, is sometimes not available.
It makes it sound as if in this vast country of ours there are retail stores in every community in Canada just waiting, begging to take over the post office. That is not the case in my riding. There are many communities in my riding that do not even have a store. They are very, very rural. The houses are five and six miles apart. I will finished in a moment Mr. Speaker.
In my community of Castalia and Grand Manan, there is a very good example of that. A business person went out and actually took over the old post office and put his own neck on the line simply to bring service to his own people, with a very strong chance of not succeeding in the marketplace. Rural Canadians deserve that service, one which Canada Post simply ignores.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite delighted to join in this debate today and speak to the motion that was put by my colleague, the hon. member for Essex-Kent, who has really studied this dossier in a very thorough manner and has brought this to the attention of our caucus enabling us to have this discussion on the motion which reads:

May 31, 1991

only for Canada Post but also for the government opposite.
The member for Essex-Kent worked very hard on the Canada Post file, ensuring that postal services are in the interest of all Canadians. I believe he has been quite instrumental in arranging to have some help extended through Canada Post and the Department of Communications to weekly newspapers for a short period of time, particularly in the code 2 category, which I will come to a little later on. I think we can all appreciate the Minister of Communications having extended this amount of money. I have the sense that it was the 13 weekly newspapers in his own riding which might have had some impact.
I suggest to all weekly newspaper owners and all citizens who live in all parts of Canada to go and talk to your member of Parliament. Bug them so that if they are on the government side, they will bug the minister and if they are on this side they will insist that the minister do something about it. Sometimes it works, not always.
The daily newspaper in your constituency is a very important asset to keeping you in touch with what is going on in the world around you. Putting that moratorium on for nine months may be fine right now, but how are we going to keep up to date and know what is going on in the future? I think we have some very shortsighted policies which do not take into account the nature of Canada, the fact that we are a country with enormous geography. This has to be thought about when we look at public policy.
Since this government has come to office it has done nothing but see to the dismantling of the ties that link Canadians across this land from coast to coast to coast and the national symbols that help us identify as Canadians. It seems to fail to understand that in order to develop this immense country, services were established to link the regions to create a sense of national unity. The need for transportation led to the birth of Air Canada and the railway.
As our fundamental communicating link, Canada Post was put into place to serve individuals, unite Canadians and enable businesses and communities to be helped nation-wide.

I know there is the argument that that continues under the privatized Canada Post. I would suggest that they did not have to privatize Canada Post in order to have an efficient service. Believe me, it is not only the private sector that is known to be efficient at all times.
I tell them to take a good look at Teleglobe under Jean-Claude Delorme and tell me that it was not functioning as well, if not better. If it was not, how come they named him to head the Caisse de depots. Don't give me the argument that only the private sector knows how to work, because it does not. There are plenty of fine public servants in the public sector. I can see one who was in the public sector before. They gave a great deal to their country and to their province and to the land internationally. They did not have to be in the private sector to be good. There is lots of reason to be very proud.
The need for transportation across this vast land, whether it was Air Canada, whether it was our bus transportation system, whether it was VIA Rail, was important to maintain that sense of Canadian identity, that linking of business and individuals across this land and to keep Canadians informed.
The CBC was also created to become a vital source of news, information and entertainment. That too was a celebrated cultural institution until this government started to cut it to pieces.
There are a lot of things government members have done that make me wonder if they really are Canadians. Canadians have long been associated with all these links. Therefore, the privatization, the closures and the downsizing that have taken place give everyone in this country a sense of abandonment, a sense of not belonging. As everybody knows, if we look at some of the cartoons, we need a sense of belonging. That loss of symbols, the loss of identity, the loss of national unity and the lack of sense of identification have led to and exacerbated the constitutional discussions we have had up till now.
I think one has to realize that in the privatization of Canada Post its business plan of action-the organ-o-gram and that it will do this, that and the other in these number of steps-may be fine and dandy, but it forgot a few human dimensions. One example is that we now have two classes of Canadian citizens: Canadian citizens who get door-to-door service and Canadian citizens who have to walk in snow, sleet, rain or ice; it does not matter what the temperature. It seems to forget that we live in the northern hemisphere. Senior citizens find it a little

May 31, 1991
Supply
bit difficult to walk down to the comer or over the icy, bumpy street to their green postal boxes, those friendly little boxes that the dogs like but not people. I would also suggest that that was not taken into consideration.
Since 1986, Canada Post has been following its corporate plan to close or convert rural and small community post offices. In 1986 there were 5,221 such post offices employing 10,000 people. Today, more than 900 have been closed or have been converted, with over 3,000 jobs lost.
What is most interesting as we look at ghettos in which people work, is that most of the workers in these rural post offices were women-83 per cent. I wonder if that had anything to do with the corporate plan.
In the coming summer there will be 156 more post offices closed in rural Canada, 12 of them in Quebec. Cela ne fait aucune logique.
The government tells me that postal rates did not really go up. All I know is that when I speak to people in my riding, when I walk into the post office and there are people standing there buying stamps, they are complaining. They lay out 43 cents for the stamp. They are not standing there calculating that the stamp was 39 cents, which was exorbitant in the first place, and that the GST has added the additional amount. They now pay 43 cents, which is a 10.5 per cent increase.
All they know is that they are paying more money. I do know that the GST is something they hate. All I would have to do if I want to fan the flames and be very partisan-I often do-would be to say: "Just blame the GST and blame those Conservatives who had such a wonderful fiscal plan for Canada. They are bleeding us dry".
Last Saturday, The Toronto Star carried a story which led off with the following words: "Every 11 days since the beginning of 1990, a Canadian magazine has folded its covers and winked out of existence." In fact, here is the story. It did not have to be on the floor, but it sure floored a lot of people in the magazine industry.
The Great Depression, two world wars, a small, spread out population, recessions, inflation, overwhelming competition from the United States; none of these killed Canadian magazines in total, but this government's lack of action is going to do that.
Why is this happening? First, because the government cut $110 million from the traditional postal subsidy that was created at the time of Confederation. We created things in this country, and the first thing you did within eight years is that you killed it. What went on here is absolutely disgraceful. For more than 100 years, governments believed it was important for all Canadians to have access to magazines, books and newspapers. Why? Because I would suggest to you that words represent ideas, transmit values and are the cornerstone of democracy.
What have we done? We have cut the postal subsidies, we added GST and we are taxing knowledge. We are taxing brains, the Bible, the Koran-what does it matter-and we have added a postal subsidy that is just going to be the final straw on the camel's back.
Studies have demonstrated the necessity of postal subsidies over decades. From the 1961 Royal Commission on Publications which is often referred to as the O'Leary commission report, to the special Senate committee on the mass media to the government's own independent studies in the 1980s, they have come to the same conclusion, that Canadian magazines face harsh economic realities. They have a very small market and very stiff U.S. competition.
We know we do not own our cultural market, that which enables our children to grow and learn for the future and remain identified strongly as Canadians.
Second, they said Canadian magazines foster in Canadians a sense of themselves in a way quite different from other media. It is true that what you see on the television screen has great impact and that an image carries 1,000 words. If you want to have that integrated into your thought process, have food for thought or sort of mull matters over in your mind, when it says: "You do not have to do it, you have a choice," and things like that such as philosophic ideas too, you have to read it and be able to re-read it.
May 31, 1991

It was interesting to note that there is no concern on the part of this government about keeping its population educated and informed through the kind of reading material that often is easier than the thick tome book or no access to a public library. They got this through their magazines.
In the pre-election period, it is very interesting with this government. In 1988, the government sort of changed its mind. I would suggest that the former communications minister Flora MacDonald had finally to admit that postal subsidies had helped to develop the publishing business and she rightly argued for the maintenance of the postal subsidy. She acknowledged that the ultimate beneficiaries of magazines and newspapers, community newspapers, trade newspapers, those newspapers which touch on ethical values, religious values, all had a good Canadian readership and were especially important to readers of small publications, readers in remote areas and readers with little access to other means of distribution.
On April 14, the minister announced: "My cabinet colleagues agreed with me that the postal subsidy is well worth preserving. Therefore, I am pleased to announce today that, for at least the next five years, the program's funding will be maintained at approximately its current level of $220 million annually."
But with the election won and the free trade agreement passed, the government broke its promise and axed the historic over-100-year-old subsidy by $110 million.
Add to this the drop in demand because of the government's 7 per cent goods and services tax. Just imagine the damage on an industry that had never been taxed before and which only had a 2 per cent profit margin. Magazines were exempt from federal manufacturers' sales tax, which the GST supposedly replaced. Therefore, there was no trade-off for the magazine industry, it was just a new tax. It was a fresh tax burden on an industry that only works on a 2 per cent profit margin.
Canadian magazine editor Doug Bennett says that the impact of this has been "the folding of 47 magazines". The industry has predicted that as the pre-GST subscriptions expire, the picture will get much worse.
You can add to that, as the article says so eloquently, the other threat that is posed by the GST, says Mrs. Keechy who is a director in the magazine industry, the inadvertent advantage it gives to the American maga-
Supply
zines which dominate the Canadian market. Strictly speaking, American publishers are supposed to collect the GST from Canadian subscribers and then remit that sum to the Canadian government. In the case of large magazines that are well known, I am sure they are doing that. But for hundreds and hundreds of smaller foreign publishers, the GST is something they just ignore and government enforcement is a complete joke. The net effect is that the Canadian magazines pay the GST while many American magazines get around it and can do business much more cheaply than we can. That certainly has not helped the industry.
With the closing of post offices, with the cutting of the postal subsidy, our cultural industries have been impacted in a very negative way. The O'Leary Royal Commission on Publications observed in 1961 that periodicals can provide "the critical analysis, the informed discourse and dialogue which are indispensable in a sovereign society". Other support mechanisms were also created.
Bill C-58 amended the Income Tax Act to encourage advertisers to use Canadian media to reach the Canadian public. Its intent is to encourage advertisers to use the Canadian media to reach that Canadian public. As a result, the measure discourages foreign ownership in Canadian periodical and newspaper publishing. To be defined as Canadian, a publication must have at least 75 per cent Canadian ownership, and 80 per cent of its material must originate in Canada. That is very helpful for our artists and our creators and many other industries in Canada. Canadian publications attribute a great deal of their success to the effects of this legislation.
There have been rumours of late from American trade officials that they would like to see the removal of Bill C-58. They find it an irritant. Well, there are so many irritants going on here that we don't need the Americans to add to the irritants, so the Americans should stay at home, mind their own business, and we will do what we need to do here, which includes putting back the postal subsidy. Mr. Treasury Board, Mr. Finance, Mr. Dollar Bills; put some money back in, and take the tax off books.
My conclusion, with respect to this whole issue and situation, Mr. Speaker, is the following: When you have postal rates that have gone up-just let me put this into the hopper-for the average newspaper weighing 107 grams, the yearly average postage costs were $2,000 up to June of this year. Costs after June will jump to $10,500 from $2,000. That is this government's wonderful way of encouraging our community newspapers, our weekly

May 31, 1991
Supply
newspapers, the ethnic papers, the church papers, the trade papers, the small daily papers. Enough is enough! Put the post offices back in rural Canada. Allow the people to have equal service. There are not two sets of citizens in this country. And, for goodness sakes, reinstate their postal service.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to express my views on the services provided by Canada Post in my riding. I will also let you know what I think of the remarkable progress this corporation has made since 1984.
While supporting the overall plan of Canada Post, I agree that, as a government agency, it has social responsibilities of a nature other than philanthropic, cultural or sports related. Canada Post could, for instance, offer very special rates to community newspapers delivered by mail to their suscribers so that people living is remote rural areas have access to quality information at a reasonable cost.
Of course, I was very happy to hear that the subsidy has been reinstated until 1992 to allow the Community Newspapers Association to determine with Canada Post how to ensure that they can go on mail delivering their weekly newspapers at a low cost. In my riding, in Lachute in particular, it was a question of life or death for the Watchman, a newspaper serving the anglophone community.
With the assistance of the Revue de la Petite-Nation, in the regional county municipality of Papineau, we were able to prove, through a rather elaborate process, Mr. Speaker, that the service was too slow in our area because of transfers made at the sorting stations. So, the Papineau area was particularly disadvantaged by this. It is much better than it was, but there is still room for improvement there. Unjustifiable delays can still be

May 31, 1991
Supply
experienced, Mr. Speaker, as I did myself last week. A letter took 10 days to get from Lachute to Mirabel.
Mr. Speaker, another major change took place. The sorting that used to be done in Lachute is now done in Saint-Jerome and Montreal, not without some backlash. I was told once again that this was a further step towards improving the service. This is a new policy. People expect mail to be delivered very quickly. Users are no longer concerned about where the sorting is handled. What they are concerned about is the cheques and letters they are expecting and they want to get them quickly.
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post is supposedly making profits now. It should consider reinvesting some of this in mail boxes. The green boxes are pretty ugly. As I was travelling through my riding I noticed, particularly in the Huberdeau area, in Harrington, these horrible green boxes on the side of the road. I think that, if Canada Post is serious about wanting to keep improving its image, that is definitely something that should be changed. Some changes are expected and more money should be put in there. Initially, the super boxes were unpopular, but I think that since people started using them the demand has grown.
Mr. Speaker, we have been advised that the Pointe-Calumet post office will close down. It was built in 1985. I think it is slightly premature to close it, considering it has just been built. However, I know the local people are working on it, and I personally advised Canada Post of my concern about this transfer which I don't think is necessary.
On the the other hand, in Saint-Colomban, things went according to plan; the office is now operating very well.
Before discussing the many improvements Canada Post has introduced, I would like to again state my support for the Association des editeurs de la press hebdomadaire regional et francophone and its fight against Admail. The association claims that Canada Post is competing unfairly with Quebec's weeklies, because Canada Post has access to over 10 million addresses across Canada, has direct access to the mailboxes of private citizens, uses its own facilities for delivery and makes a substantial profit in areas where it has a monopoly.
Personally, I think the director of the federal Bureau of Competition Policy should deal with this matter once and for all and conduct an investigation to see whether this Crown corporation is unlawfully competing with regional weekly newspapers.
Perhaps we could now look at the progress made by this corporation which today has annual revenues of nearly $4 billion. Every day, about 40 million items deposited at 750,000 points of mailing are processed and then delivered to any of more than 11 million addresses in this country or sent to countries all over the world.
Contrary to what is commonly thought, Canada Post does not have a monopoly on mail delivery in Canada. Letter mail, which is only 50 per cent of its business, is the only area over which it has a monopoly, by law. Even in that market, Canada Post has to compete with fax machines which have now become a direct and very effective means of communication. You get your mail in minutes, not days. So the fax machine has become a serious competitor for Canada Post. There is also electronic information and fund transfer networks and, of course, the telephone.
Other products and services, like priority post and parcel delivery, are areas where competition by courier firms, bus or truck companies, airlines, advertising media and other businesses involved in delivery of communications is very fierce. However, that is how the free enterprise system works, and Canada Post is now part of that system. So now they have to act like a company, and not like a Crown corporation that can knock on the door of the Minister of Finance to get some money because it didn't make enough the year before. It cannot operate like that anymore. So, the company has to make its products competitive and meet the market demands.
Canada Post also has to fight every inch of the way to keep its share of the market and it may be that, in part, that irritates and brings opposition from the community newspapers. On the other hand, it must be said in its defence that Canada Post is a company and must act as such.
At the Ottawa headquarters, a national control centre was set up to ensure the proper operation of the entire system and monitor the daily mail flow. It is from that centre that Canada Post coordinates the activities of its
May 31, 1991

57,000	employees and 12,000 suppliers with those of the contract carriers, large volume mailers, small businesses it deals with as well as all its clients.
In that centre, screens allow the continual monitoring of air transportation and weather conditions throughout the country. In fact, all members of this House and anyone interested to see how it works should go and visit the center. It is great to see how mail flow is controlled in Canada. Other terminals are used to analyse the volume of mail entering or leaving of the system. On another wall, twelve screens provide an up-to-the-minute picture of the progress of mail through the company's network of handling plants.
The national centre is linked to nine regional control centre from coast to coast by state-of-the-art telecommunication and data processing systems. There, a Canada Post senior management team meets every morning and, there also, inquiries regarding the operation of the network are relayed instantly for the appropriate person to respond to immediately.
The history of the modern-day Canada Post Corporation started in 1981. So, when we hear the Liberals and their great philosophies, we must remember it started under them. They know very well that, were they sitting on this side of the House, they would be saying the exact same things as I do today. That is the beauty of the parliamentary system. Because they are sitting on the other side, we can do nothing right; but if they were sitting on this side, then I would be in the opposition and perhaps I would be doing the same thing. The fact remains that they started this in 1981. Because we set up the new postal corporation, it does not work since the Liberals did not do it. Anyway, things are much better when the Conservatives do it. Is that not so, Mr. Speaker?
Postal service had become less and less reliable. Strikes deprived Canadians of postal service for weeks; the deficit had grown to $600 million a year and was on its way to $1 billion. Listen, a deficit of $1 billion in 1981! Imagine how much it would cost to mail a letter today if we had done nothing. It would be frightful!
It was a completely unacceptable burden for taxpayers. I hope that those listening to us today agree with me.
Supply
Many postal establishments were inefficient and much of the equipment was becoming obsolete. Obviously, with a billion-dollar deficit, how can you buy new equipment? It is impossible, is it not? You have to pay back the deficit. But successive governments had other more urgent needs to meet with their limited resources than investing in capital equipment for the Post Office.
In that context, a quarter of the Public Service suddenly became a commercial business. What a change! The new corporation had more than 63,000 full-and parttime employees, but no infrastructure like labour relations, legal services, finance, purchasing and so on-indeed, everything that a normal business or any company needs to run properly.
All those functions were performed by all kinds of other departments. The new company had an annual volume of over $1.5 billion, but-get this-no bank account! It carried on its activities all across Canada but it had no control over them. The nine years since that shaky start are divided into three phases: in the first phase, from 1981 to 1985, the corporation built up the infrastructure essential for any business. Just to let my colleague on the other side know, we were elected in 1984. Things had begun to deteriorate four years earlier, even if you would want us to believe otherwise. Canada Post was restructured according to business management principles. Of course, they had to get competent people from the private sector. Financial statements had to be prepared and all the support services a big business would need had to be put in place. New goals were defined, resources were assessed, prepared, and a five-year plan established, just to name a few innovations.
In 1985, we were in office when Canada Post management realized they were dead wrong in believing they knew how to operate a postal service. After all, that is what they had been doing for over a hundred years. They were wrong, Mr. Speaker. That year, they lost control and did not know how to react. Consequently, the second stage of the restructurization was never planned, it just happened out of necessity. Between 1986 and 1989, Canada Post did not release any public statement. They closed down their marketing service. What they wanted was to start to standardize their operations throughout the country. That is when they implemented a system-

Supply
ized process, with national standards of service they could control and measure.
To regain some of their credibility and prove their reliability, they made some fundamental changes in then-system, Mr. Speaker, and I insist on the word "fundamental". First, they eliminated their first-class, second-class, and third-class mail service, as if there could be different classes of customers. They are all first-class users. A business must have only first-class products.
The corporation negotiated some flexibility in its collective agreements, to improve service efficiency. I believe that most of the people now working for the Canada Post Corporation are proud of what has been accomplished and I am not sure that, should you ask them, Mr. Speaker, they would agree to return to the old Post Office Department.
Productivity has improved greatly. The Corporation asked for guarantees of performance from its suppliers of air and road transportation. It was an obvious choice. It is not insignificant, since Canada Post is the largest buyer of transportation services in Canada. It is perfectly logical to ask for quality service. It put in place preferred rates for large volume customers who agree to prepare their mail and deliver it to the carrier. It invested in the best equipment and technological system. It consistently sought to integrate this system with the ones used by companies, since 80 per cent of the mail it processes comes from corporate customers.
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post is the first postal administration in the world to have its productivity measured by an independent auditor and to make public the results of such an exercise. The quarterly reports show a constant improvement in the performance of the corporation from an average of less than 85 per cent, according to the first reports issued back in 1987.
I regret that my colleague from Glengariy-Prescott- Russell, just the other side of the bridge from my riding- Usually, when I speak, he is in the House. I wish he were here for I could have given him the results of a mini poll carried out in Hawkesbury. People in Hawkes-buiy were asked: Is the mail service any better? I said it in English, because that is the way it was reported in the paper. One person answered:

"I am happy with the mail delivery here in Hawkesbury. I have not noticed much of a change. It is always the same. The service is good."
Another wrote: "Yes, the service has definitely improved. I use the post office quite a lot and I am pleased with the service. I think they are doing a fine job".

And I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker.
So, about three years ago, Canada Post Corporation turned a profit in accordance, of course, with its corporate plans. Any business who does not turn a profit has to close shop. It's a fact. Since becoming a business concern, the corporation must show a profit. There's no getting around it. Only the New Democrats do not understand that a business must earn money.
It was the first year in the black, and the first time that Canada Post made a profit in 30 years. With that started Phase III. The corporation was now able to show a different image to Canadians. So, in 1989, it had its first profit of $96 million dollars. The corporation had gone from a $600 million deficit, almost one billion, to a $96 million profit. They must have thought: Good, now we can buy ourselves some machinery.
The next year, the corporation did even better: profits of $149 million, at the same time as it improved service, let us not forget! Surveys were done. People do not complain about the service. When a change is made, it takes two or three weeks. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we are always attached to our services and reluctant to change-that is quite normal. But after three weeks or a month, people realize that it is not so bad. People go to pick up their mail at any time of the day. People work today, both partners in a couple work and it is not always convenient to go to the post office by one o'clock or between three and four- Today, they can pick up their mail much longer and take advantage of the services.
Imagine, Mr. Speaker-this must be horrible for any socialist-Canada Post Corporation paid the federal government a $60-million dividend! You, ladies and gentlemen, you taxpayers, after paying through your taxes for years to subsidize a deficit, received a $60-million dividend paid to the government! The corporation invests $400 million a year on average in equipment,
May 31, 1991

training, new technology to improve services and Canada Post has thus become a world leader in postal high technology. This is possible because the corporation is profitable; if it were not, it could not invest in new technologies.
The new postal system comes into play from the very beginning of the development of a marketing or billing concept in any of the businesses which provide Canada Post with 80 percent of the volume of mail it handles over the year.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt about it-I have encountered it myself, as all members of this House have, I am sure; I encounter it every day in my riding- there is a normal resistance to change in services from our constituents. Just a little while ago, a meeting was held in Pointe-Calumet and people went and said maybe we should have done things this way or another way. At least, Canada Post takes the time to consult the people and to listen to them. There is a 90-day period set aside for consultation. In the end, the people come to realize that the corporation's plans are not all that bad. It takes a little time, but in the end they are satisfied. And the superboxes, Mr. Speaker, they are just great!
I would like to say, in closing, that I too, as a taxpayer and a member of Parliament, am happy to see the corporation paying us dividends, allowing us thereby to improve services and, of course, to apply that money toward the reduction of the deficit and finally to increase the services provided to Canadians.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I found the hon. member's speech somewhat confusing, because at first she said she supported and agreed with Canada Post's corporate plan. That she started to say: You know, this doesn't work very well, and that service could be improved- Although she agreed with this plan, she was against letting Canada Post operate in areas where it would be competing with private businesses, such as regional weeklies.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member does not understand the real problem. Today, we are talking about Canada Post, but we could just as well be talking about Air Canada, the CBC, VIA Rail- It's the whole philosophy of a government that says the market is always right. It is a matter of making money, making a profit, and the government isn't interested in the citizens of this country
Supply
or in providing a service for Canadians. Earlier, the hon. member mentioned auditors who were supposed to measure the performance of our postal services. We all know about the surveys at Canada Post, Mr. Speaker. I was a critic for two years.
And a very good critic!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Every time we took a closer look at the figures, we realized it was all planned so they could say: We conducted a survey, the people agree, and now we can close the post office in their community.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should look at the real story. In 1984, when this government came to power, the first thing the Minister of Finance told Canada Post was: As of 1985, you will have to balance your books, but you can't compete with private enterprise. Now listen, it doesn't take a genius to realize that the only thing they could do was cut services.
So they went and closed a whole bunch of post offices in rural areas. They installed superboxes before they put up the green boxes, and now, of course, as the hon. member said, people prefer the superboxes. Mr. Speaker, of course they are better than the green boxes, which are a real disgrace, as the hon. member said.
However, in urban areas, people keep asking us for home delivery, not those superboxes. Mr. Speaker, I live here in Gatineau and I have a superbox. Every morning when I open my box, it's full of junk mail. That is what we have now, Mr. Speaker!
We have a mailbox for all the advertising they sent us. And what do people want? They want service. The government can talk about money and profits-of course Canada Post is making a profit. The government also says everyone is satisfied with the service, but, Mr. Speaker-and I refer now to the Rimouski area-I could show the hon. member hundreds of thousands of petitions these people are sending in. If you want to see people who are against Canada Post- Earlier I mentioned the Archbishop of Rimouski, and I could read a few more names: I have here Father Pascal Parent, the parish priest; the parish of Sainte-Blandine; the Association feminine d'education d'action sociale- You want to hear some more names of people who don't agree? Gilles Roy, vice-president of the Urgence rurale coalition. You want more names? Well, I will give you some more: the Ficelle organization, MPPs, Mayor Daniel

May 31, 1991
Supply
Cote, MPP Michel Tremblay, all from a rural area around Rimouski.
Thousands of people are up in arms, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member says everybody is happy with the service they are getting. Mr. Speaker, the truth is, we are not getting any service in this country. Everything has been cut.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the archbishop of Rimouski is interested in what is going on in his community, but I am also sure that the archbishop would be the first to realize that Canada Post must ensure that the customer who wants service has to be dealt with efficiently.
They say that post offices have been shut down. Granted, some post offices have been shut down, but service was transferred to small businesses in the same community. Yes, the post office has been closed, but the service was transferred elsewere. The guy to whom you address a letter as "John Doe, St. Blandine, County of Rimouski" will get his letter, his mail.
At the archbishop's palace!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if it is going to be the archbishop who will receive it, but, as the member for Saint-Denis said, Joe Blow, Sainte-Blan-dine, Rimouski County will get his mail.
So, when they say that post offices were closed, they are exaggerating a little. The services were transferred, and I can tell you that in several small communities, there are businesses like convenience stores that are open until 11 at night where many constituents go to get their mail and buy a few things at the same time to encourage those small shopkeepers.
Sure, before that, we used to have post offices with postmasters and all that in every community. You know, Mr. Speaker, in some municipalities, when the Liberals formed the government, post offices were built everywhere. There was one on this side of the road, and another on the other side. The postmaster on one side said hello to the one on the other side. They even asked questions of each other to know at what time they would-That really happened in a community, the name of which I have forgotten.
If it was politically rewarding, post offices were built. It was like during the Duplessis days, bridges were built where there was no water. So, let us not exaggerate. The service was upgraded. I understand people who are against it, but, once again, everyone gets his mail, though in different ways.

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member says that everything is fine today, I cannot help thinking about my responsabilities towards my riding. I want to tell her, for example, that in the new modem life, perhaps in the new big developments, and I say only perhaps-But she knows my riding very well, since, under the previous government, from 1984 to 1988, she was the hon. member responsible for the riding of Saint-Denis, to see who could defeat the member for Saint-Denis. But I must admit that she is an excellent friend.
It is absurd to see that in the Bois-de-Boulogne, which is very well known, in Montreal-I am not talking about the Bois-de-Boulogne in Paris, but the one in Montreal, which is a residential area-there are people in the north, the east, the west and the south; so they are completely surrounded, but there are also a few developments in some streets. For example, I am thinking of Marcellin-Wilson Street. I am thinking of a whole new estate belonging to Mr. Fiori. I am thinking of the new estate of the people she knows well, like Mr. Musto. In the heart of the city of Montreal, new streets were built to connect with others, and superboxes were installed. In the winter, there is a lot a snow and ice. Older people are now scared to go there. Well, it is the people who bought estates at $400,000 or $500,000 who get all the promotional mail that they do not want. This is the new way for Canada Post to manage a good department, always in the name of sound management! I find it is sad. I must admit-this is a rare occurence and I want to soothe my colleague, Mr. Cooper, with whom I had an exchange that I regret a bit-that there were some exaggerations. II you tell me that everything is fine, I think that you do not believe it. I point out that the member seems to be of the same opinion. But there were some unfortunate incidents.
As the member for Saint-Denis, I simply wanted to submit a case that happened in my riding, in one of the completely or almost completely built areas where,
May 31, 1991

between two streets, they built a half-street on which people cannot even find the services that are available to their neighbours.
So, it is not a new area, a new development, a new city, or a new village. It is right in the middle of Montreal between two streets, because it was built later.
Therefore, I would hope that she joins with me to make representations to Canada Post to begin correcting what appears to me to be great anomalies.
