speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have a chance to join in some debate today on this very important motion that we have before us regarding postal service in Canada, dealing with Canada Post.
I just want to read the motion into the record:
That this House call upon the government to institute policies that
would require that service to Canadians be the priority for Canada
Post.
That is a very important motion for us to be debating today. As is evidenced by the debate we have had in this chamber today, there are members on all sides of this House, on this side and on the government side as well, who have some very specific and important concerns about the way Canada Post is operating.
There is, as well, a particular interest among those members who represent rural ridings about some of the problems that we have had in our dealings with Canada Post in those communities.

May 31, 1991
Supply
Before I start my comments, I would just like to say a couple of things. First, I would like to pay credit to two of my colleagues who have done a considerable amount of work in this particular area.
Our previous post office critic, the member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, did a great deal of work in this area. He gained some recognition by producing a major report for our caucus. The member for Churchill, who is our current postal critic-I thank him for providing some notes-is unable to be with us in the debate today. Given the size of his riding, he also has some particular concerns about Canada Post.
There are two other groups of people who I hope are watching and listening to the debate today. The first is ordinary Canadians. Almost all Canadians have the opportunity to interface with Canada Post and to deal with that Crown corporation. I hope Canadians are listening today to see some of the concerns being raised by members of Parliament and to see, as well, that even on the government backbenches there is concern about how the corporation is running.
There is one other group, too, that I hope is paying attention. These are the people who are watching in the control room at Canada Post headquarters right now. I hope they are watching this debate, that they are taking notes on all of the concerns that have been raised here.
I trust that as a responsible Crown corporation Canada Post will take the effort to follow up on those concerns that were raised and attempt to address them and help us to assist our constituents.
I would like to take a brief look and make some comments about what this government has allowed Canada Post to do nationally and the direction in which it is going. Then I would like to make some comments about my dealings with Canada Post in my riding and, to conclude, make some comments on some of the recommendations that the New Democratic Party caucus has made and some that I have made, to ensure that Canada Post is a successful Crown corporation.
Clearly, the record speaks for itself; the main focus of Canada Post under the Conservative government has been to close or to turn over and privatize retail postal outlets and post offices in Canada.
In fact, a lot of the information that I have been provided with comes from an organization that has arisen in the past couple of years and which deserves some credit from this House. It is an organization called Rural Dignity. It has done an outstanding job across Canada raising concerns, primarily about post offices, but as well about VIA Rail and other services as it impacts on small communities.
I did not bring it with me today-I should have-but Rural Dignity is raising funds by selling a poster depicting a rural scene. That is a plug for anyone who is interested in picking up one of those posters. I have ordered one. I think the importance and contribution that rural Canada makes is an important part of Canada and one that we have often missed in this debate in this Chamber.
The figures are incredible. Over 1,000 rural post offices have been closed or privatized since 1986 and some 3,000 full-and part-time jobs have been lost. Over 200 communities are now without any kind of replacement postal service. In many cases, this has meant a reduction of the federal presence in Canada.
Many in my province of British Columbia are familiar with a position called "the government agent", someone who in a smaller community is really a catch-all for provincial government services and a very important person. Often in many small communities that was what the post office was. It was the federal government agent, the place people could go to get their income tax forms, GRIP forms and other paperwork when people need it from the federal government. The closing of these post offices has meant that we have lost that.
That is not even to mention the economic impact these closures have had on many small communities. Magazines and other publications have commented on the large number of people who are now running small businesses out of their basements on the side, who quite often depend on the post office to deliver their product or service. We are seeing a great deal of that now and the loss of many of these rural post offices has really hurt them.
As well, there is the absolute lack of consultation with those communities by Canada Post. One example that struck me, which was an important one, and it goes back, if I have my timing right, to last summer to a major debate in, I believe, the Westwold area of British Columbia. Canada Post usually moves pretty fast if a
May 31, 1991

postmaster dies or retires. I hope the postmasters in my riding do not choose to pass on soon. Then you can really get the mail moving fast, because Canada Post moves like greased lightning as soon as a postmaster dies or retires. It moves in very quickly, either to close the operation down or to try and privatize it.
A revealing comment was made in a discussion I had with Canada Post officials in Vancouver-and I am not suggesting in this case that they lied to me, but it is as bad as if they had. I phoned and this person said: "Well, since we"-meaning Canada Post-"eventually won this battle with the community of Westwold"-where they chained up the Canada Post vehicle, wrote letters and raised a great deal of concern, with the help of the member for Kamloops-"since the management of our corporation did not back down and since the government did not step in to make a decision, we figure we can go ahead and do anything we want and we know we have the backing of our management". It was a very revealing comment. It says that in many cases, when these staff members are doing what they are told, which is to close or privatize a post office, they are likely to go all the way.
I know in talking to my colleague, our previous postal critic, that you win a few but you wonder just how much you have won.
In today's paper there is a report of many letters that we have received from people of Mabou, Cape Breton who feel they have won an interim victory in getting the post office to back down. I hope that is right. I hope they have won a victory over Canada Post. If they have, I think we should circulate their letters and these articles in the newspapers to everybody so that all members of Parliament, when Canada Post is moving in to close down a service, can use the experience of these courageous people in Cape Breton, who have fought and, so far, have won. I suppose we will have to wait and see just what the final outcome of this particular fight will be.
The final outcome may be the next federal election, when we get rid of the Conservatives and elect the New Democrats and bring in a postal policy that will be relevant in this country.
Supply
One of the problems that has arisen in the postal service as it is being run by Canada Post now, with the turnover to the retail postal outlets, is that they say: "We are not closing the post office, we are going to turn it over to an entrepreneur to run in their drugstore or their motel, or what have you". That has resulted in problems. A woman phoned my office this morning, knowing I would be rising in debate today on the post office, just commenting on a few things such as the lack of universal hours, something we know we need when dealing with the post office, and different advice on mailing. This woman was particularly upset. She wanted to write a letter to the Prime Minister to complain about the Prime Minister's partisan attitude while abroad. The person to whom she went to mail her letter did not know that one could still mail letters free of charge to the Prime Minister and other members of Parliament.
It is an inconsistent service that we have. The need for a professional service has been one of the most important messages that I have received from officials in Canada Post when I travelled throughout my riding. I have done that as I am sure have many other members of Parliament.
As a new member I have visited just about all of the postal outlets in Prince George-Bulkley Valley, talked to staff, management, employees and others to get a sense of where they are going and to introduce myself. It has been a learning experience because in most cases the staff in the postal outlets are dedicated people, especially in the rural communities. They are dedicated to their jobs. They want to provide good service, but they certainly wonder what the control room in head office is doing. I wonder what the control room in the cabinet offices and the Government of Canada are doing right now.
I told the letter carriers and the inside workers that I would be going on a postal walk with a letter carrier this summer and doing a bit of work inside the post office to get a better understanding of what they have to deal with. That is important, I have learned from some of my discussions with postmasters and postal employees. In particular, I discussed this with some postal workers last night, knowing I would be speaking today.
One example in Prince George is a new program Canada Post is bringing in called the "Lead Hand Program". It will essentially take out the management

Supply
and supervisory person and generally turn over the paperwork which always has to be done to the lead hand person. Such persons also have a job at the counter or the wicket. They should be spending a third or half of their day at the wicket serving customers, but they will have to sit down, fill out and complete all the paperwork.
It is my view, which I think is shared by a lot of people, that it is a deliberate move by Canada Post, especially in my case in Prince George, Station A, Fifth Avenue, to have the service deteriorate to the point where Canada Post will have to say that it has many complaints, that service has gone down hill, and that there is nothing to be done except either privatize or close the post office and let the drug store nearby serve the area.
There is an overtime ban now so that the mail which should go out that day does not always do so. It gets bumped to the next day or perhaps even to the following day. There is a good deal of concern when people do not get their mail on time. That is another reason why that would happen.
There are around a hundred grievances alone out of the Prince George area. I get anonymous letters about once a month from staff who work in that area and are concerned. Of course I pass these on to both management and union for them to pursue.
I have had my own experience in my riding with the closing of post offices in two cases. First, the community of Endako assumed it was going to happen and there was not much it could do. The second was the community of Longworth where I met with a number of residents very concerned about losing their postal service. That community does not have phones either, and in this case I offered to try at least to pass some information on to Canada Post so that it would know where Longworth was. We did not suspect that anyone from Canada Post had ever actually been to Longworth. With no telephones, we also told Canada Post that if it is going to have its community meeting, it is going to have to write a letter to tell the community when it is going to come, because Canada Post does not know that community very well. It is someone in Vancouver who is making the decision to close this outlet, because a postmaster in that particular postal service is retiring. As I said, if you are a postmaster and you die in office or you retire in office,
you can be assured that Canada Post will move with lightning speed.
What should be done? We have to maintain Canada Post as a public Crown corporation at the very least. I have a great deal of fear, and I think a lot of Canadians do, that this government is fattening up Canada Post so it can privatize the whole operation.
Then you will see how much it costs to mail a letter from Granisle to Vancouver. You are going to be charged about $5 just to mail a letter if it is privatized under the Conservatives.
We want to make sure that we do not exclude letter carrier service from recently developed communities, in particular older areas that are being rebuilt. Canada Post moves very quickly. You get a superbox thrown up in your face as soon as a new area is developed so that it trims back the letter carrier service.
In Britain, I understand the post office has had a different history. It has provided many more services. Our Canada Post has experimented with some services with, I believe, some degree of success, and not so with others. I think it could do a great deal more in terms of not just its fax business, where you fax something and it gets mailed the next day, but in terms of becoming much more of a business-type centre, and most important, in terms of maintaining the full kind of postal service to all Canadians that we have come to expect and deserve.
Some have alleged that the profit figures for Canada Post are bogus profit figures. It we are to take at face value that they are honest figures, I think it is important for Canada Post to perhaps rebuild some of the infrastructure that it has allowed to be destroyed and to return some of the integrity to the system.
I visited a motel operation which is now the postal outlet in Topley. I do know that Canada Post pays $100 or $200 a month and then a commission on stamps and postage. But I felt bad when I was leaving their little operation. I felt I should come and buy all my stamps at this location because of the meagre amount of commission the postmaster in Topley was likely to get. It was the usual case of the postmaster retiring: "Do we give it to this other business?" "No, it is not worth my while", so someone picks it up and eventually it is going to get to
May 31, 1991

the point where as an entrepreneur they cannot continue and they are going to have to close.
Certainly a review of the return of the benefits to some of these smaller outlets is one of the important things that Canada Post should do when it is reviewing the service. How do we get Canada Post to make these changes? One of the government members made the point that it is very independent now as a Crown corporation. It takes a lot to move it.
I would say that if Canada Post is not interested in returning the kind of rural service that we need in Canada, we should fire the president of Canada Post. If need be, I think we should renationalize Canada Post and bring back the kind of post office we need in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague, the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley, for his address and the particular concerns that he has outlined regarding the situation with Canada Post.
As B.C. members, my colleague and I have talked about the issue of Canada Post closures.
He is also well aware of the fact that there are postal closures occurring not only in his riding but in many ridings and constituencies throughout Canada. One of the more recent closures occurred in the town of Enderby in my constituency.
I should point out that Enderby is actually one of the largest of rural postal closures to date. There have been hundreds of rural post offices closed. If the government continues to get its way, eventually all post offices will be closed and privatized. The one in Enderby is of particular interest because of the fact that it is a very large one.
I want to address my comments to my colleague to see if he would support me in my request to the government. When the initial news of this closure came down, I wrote to the post office to request whether it would consider holding a public meeting with the residents of the Enderby area in the Okanagan-Shuswap and consider the various options.
I was really surprised, quite flabbergasted by the return comments made by Mr. Doug McClelland, Manager of Media and Community Services out of Vancouver. He essentially said: "We are not interested in the views of the community; we will make the decision and
Supply
then tell the community afterward what that decision has been."
It did make a decision: close the post office. It came up and held a public meeting. It was interesting that one of the suggestions that came out of the meeting, which was strongly supported by the community of Enderby as well as the retail community and the residents, was that a couple of Enderby residents would take over the retail operation of the post office in its present location and would continue the operations in the building which people have come to know and trust as the centre for postal services in Enderby. This was an option that Canada Post had not even thought about. I am hoping it is still pursuing that option because it makes sense to the city of Enderby in terms of the availability of service.
I am just asking if my colleague will support me in my request to the government that it seriously consider this request coming from me as well as from the residents of the community of Enderby.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the question or comment from the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap. My grandparents lived there for a while and so I know Enderby a bit.
It came as a surprise when he mentioned that Canada Post was trying to close an outlet there, a standard post office, because it is not the size of community in which you would expect Canada Post do something like that.
It seems to me it is a bit of a hidden agenda that Canada Post has. It goes through the routine, it is pro forma: "have a community meeting, yes, yes, we will listen to you. Say your bit and we will consult and figure out what we want to do." We know what it is going to do anyway, so it is a bit of a phoney dance we go through.
Perhaps what we have to do is try and make that phoney dance a little more real. Perhaps we should have the president of Canada Post attend these community meetings where it is closing post offices so that he would get a real example of just what these communities have to go through.
If the member is asking for support for a backup plan which the community might have for running a retail outlet in the post office building, I would endorse it. Canada Post has an obligation to run that service. It would seem to me that given the comments of the corporation in the past, this is something it would and

May 31, 1991
Supply
should consider. I would be quite surprised and disappointed if the corporation were not prepared to do that.
I would certainly support the member. I know he has done a great deal of work in his riding, in Vernon, in Enderby and in other areas on the postal service. I would support whatever efforts he has made in that area and we hope that Canada Post will listen intently to the needs of the residents of his community.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been an interesting debate this afternoon on the pros and cons. It is clear that the postal service in this country is changing and meeting new demands across the country and trying to stay within the bounds of regional economics rather than create enormous government debt in the post office.
It gives me pleasure to speak in the House today about the Canada Post Corporation and how it is changing to better serve Canadians to meet the challenges of the globally competitive world evolving around us.
I think the members opposite would agree that the business challenges facing Canada Post are monumental. Here is a quick overview of the corporation today and how it is adapting to meet these challenges. In terms of annual revenues, it is a $4 billion operation. With approximately 57,000 employees, it is also one of the largest employers in the country. It processes 10 billion pieces of mail a year and delivers to over 11 million addresses.
Through links with other postal administrations, it keeps Canadians in touch with every country in the world.
Over the past 10 years, this corporation has learned a lot about corporate reshaping. Its management took the government department it inherited, stripped it down to basics and rebuilt it.
This government believes Canada needs and deserves a strong postal communications system as part of its basic economic infrastructure to compete successfully domestically and globally. Equally important, we believe it must provide the Canadian public with the most reliable, cost-efficient postal communications possible.
The modem Canada Post Corporation began in 1981, when the government took some 63,000 employees-one quarter of the Canadian Public Service-and said: "Okay, post office, you are a business. Act like a commercial corporation."
The mail had become increasingly unreliable. Strikes denied Canadians their postal service for weeks at a time. Annual deficits had reached $600 million, which in today's dollars would be close to $1 billion.
Its plants were inefficient, with outdated, if not obsolete equipment. Previous governments had found more pressing needs for their limited resources than investing in capital assets for the post office.
This new Crown corporation had annual revenues of more than $1.5 billion but no bank account. It operated from one end of the country to another but no one knew where the mail was at any given time.
In order to meet the enormous task that lay ahead, Canada Post began thinking like a business. It began to emphasize a corporate culture, stressing such values as customer sensitivity, quality and reliability. These values were not easily instilled but the corporation has worked over the years to ensure that these will be values which its employees live by, day to day.
By 1986, the corporation was ready to regain credibility by providing its service reliably. It standardized operations across the country. It developed a mail processing system that had performance standards which would be monitored and measured on a real time basis.
Effectively, this made everyone accountable so that they all knew when they were doing a good job and when they were not. For the first time, it was able to thank employees for a job well done, or, conversely, talk about the need for improvement. All this was done in the name of providing better service for Canadians.
The corporation also began to demand that all suppliers and contractors meet its new business standards. The corporation now negotiates contracts with its suppliers and contractors that ensure they recognize the importance of meeting the needs and requirements of the corporation's customers.
May 31, 1991

The corporation has also hired outside auditors to measure delivery performance, the first postal administration in the world to do so. As mentioned previously by my hon. colleague, the most recent report by these auditors indicates it is now at 97 per cent efficiency.
It is no exaggeration to say that changes the corporation has undergone are staggering. It stood everything on its head, examined every process and questioned every assumption. It has had to challenge its people every day. It demanded their creativity and a complete commitment. The process was tough on everyone, from the executive offices to the plant floors. Some left, but most have soldiered on. This is a tribute to the quality of these people and they have done a fine job.
The changes have been equally tough on the unions which have had to recognize that they are in business with Canada Post. If the business fails then they both fail, but if the corporation wins as a company so does its employees and the unions who represent it. I believe union leaders must recognize that global competition applies to them too. This puts their own attitudes and productivity against those of the unions around the world.
As such, Canada Post has had to negotiate flexibility in its union contracts to increase their efficiency and re-establish management's right to manage the business. That did not come easily.
Clear evidence that the corporation's efforts were beginning to bear fruit appeared in 1988-89 when, as my hon. colleague who spoke previously mentioned, the corporation turned a profit for the first time in 30 years. This point bears repeating as taxpayers are no longer forced to pay for their postal service twice: once when they paid for their stamps and again when they paid their taxes.
This year, total mail volumes will hit some 10 billion pieces of mail. That is an increase of 38 per cent since the first full year of incorporation, and half of that was achieved in the last two years alone. Yet, Canada Post is doing all this with 6,000 fewer employees. Its mail processing efficiency also increased by approximately 6 per cent last year. That compares with the Canadian manufacturing productivity increases of less than one per cent last year.
Supply
It has been through changes such as those outlined above that Canada Post Corporation has held increases in the basic mail rate for Canadians to less than the rate of inflation since 1982-83.
Yes, Canada Post has made progress over the past 10 years, but they can feel their competitors breathing down their necks every day, not just in Canada but from around the world.
Their sales force is slugging it out with the courier businesses and the telecommunications companies. Even the basic letter mail is under threat from fax machines and new technologies such as electronic data transfer. If you have paid any bills lately using your bank machine, Mr. Speaker, you will know what I am speaking about.
To help them successfully compete, Canada Post has invested more than a billion dollars in the company in the last three years. Some of this has gone into new trucks and street letter boxes. About a quarter billion is going into new-generation sorting equipment that is faster, more accurate and more versatile, replacing equipment that is 20 years old. Some of the new equipment can process mail up to 50 per cent faster than its predecessors.
Instead of equipping the Canadian postal system with off-the-shelf technology, as occurred 20 years ago, the corporation went to the manufacturers and told them to adapt their technology to Canada Post's specifications.
For example, they built a national control centre, linked with control centres in nine divisions across the country. These control centres are equipped with the latest computer-based technology. They monitor the collection, processing and delivery networks, transportation carriers, and even the national weather office: they then can pinpoint the movement of mail anywhere in Canada, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and ensure that it moves to meet service standards.
Competition is getting tougher, not only in Canada but globally as well. Although opportunities abound out there, the business streets of the world are getting mean. All businesses have to be globally street smart if they are to prosper. As such, Canada Post has gone global in a couple of ways. The president and chief executive officer of Canada Post is also currently the chairman of the

Supply
board of the International Post Corporation, which was formed three years ago.
The corporate headquarters and operational centre for the International Post Corporation is in Brussels. It groups 23 of the world's leading postal administrations, all of whom own shares. Its primary objective is to ensure competitive service standards are met in the distribution of parcels and courier products among Europe, North America and the Pacific Rim. Even the post office can no longer be restricted by national barriers. Its competitors, the multinational courier companies, certainly are not. As such, when word about the new Canadian postal system got around to other postal administrations, they came to see how we did it. So did dozens of Canadian companies, including Canadian Airlines International, Domtar, Bell Canada, Xerox, Sears, MacLeans magazine and the Aerospace Industries Association of Canada, as well as 23 chief executive officers from major foreign companies.
In an effort to meet the growing world-wide demand for Canada Post expertise, the corporation has created a new subsidiary called Canada Post Systems Management Ltd., which has been tasked with selling its technology and management systems world-wide. I am pleased to say that it has discovered a growing market out there for the systems it put into place in Canada to get operations under control. Indeed, it has already closed a multi-million dollar deal with New Zealand Post and is implementing control systems there.
Canada Post's international reputation is such that it was recently recommended by the World Bank to Venezuela, which had approached the bank seeking assistance in upgrading its postal system. This sort of recognition by a major multinational organization like the World Bank sends a pretty clear message of the high regard in which the corporation is held internationally.
I should also add that proposals worth more than $40 million have been issued to postal administrations in Europe and Central America. This international consulting promises to be a profitable sideline, not only for Canada Post, but for many of their Canadian suppliers and partners as well.
I would like to present just one example of this. A few years ago, the corporation decided it needed a way to track and trace its priority courier parcels and envelopes through the postal system to ensure they did not go astray.
The corporation turned to SHL Systemhouse, a Canadian systems integrator. They delivered a track and trace system on time and on budget, a system that helps Priority Courier achieve its close to 100 per cent reliability for next day delivery.
Systemhouse then used its experience with Canada Post to bid on a trace system for the United States postal service. It won a $270 million U.S. contract, the largest ever won by the company. I am pleased that, through its involvement with Canada Post, this wholly-owned Canadian company was able to win such a lucrative and significant contract in the United States.
This is the sort of success story that could only be possible due to the success of the free trade agreement. It is an example of how the use of new technology by Canada Post and other Canadian companies is helping Canada win new business in information age markets.
Now, and most important, I would like to address how the corporation has been improving the products and services it provides to the Canadian public.
It moves letter mail, advertising mail, publications, courier documents and parcels. It moves facsimiles, electronic messages, or a combination of hard copy and electronic messages called hybrid mail.
It has restructured its products to meet customers' requirements for cost efficiency and reliability. It provides different speeds of delivery on a time-price scale, with add-on options such as insurance and tracing. Customers now have the ability to pick the speed and options needed, and pay accordingly.
The corporation's parcel services are now geared to the just-in-time delivery disciplines of its industrial customers, so it can minimize the capital that is tied up in inventory. It is also working with large volume mailers to show how to save money and ensure timely delivery by presorting their mail and by scheduling its arrival at its mail processing plants.
Canada Post has made these changes because business provides over 80 per cent of Canada Post's volumes and revenues. In meeting the needs of businesses, the corporation is able to generate the volumes needed to support its extensive operations network. This enables the corporation to provide all Canadians with a basic letter mail rate that remains the second lowest, in terms of minutes of labour required to earn the price of a stamp, in the western industrialized world. Indeed, since
May 31, 1991

incorporation 10 years go, the actual price of a stamp has decreased relative to inflation.
When Canada Post became a Crown corporation 10 years ago, it faced many problems that some people regarded as being impossible to resolve. It has not settled all of them, but it has achieved a fair measure of success. Direct Marketing Magazine, an American publication, recently stated: "Canada Post emerges as the model for postal services around the world. You would be astounded to see the space age technology in Ottawa which controls the flow of mail throughout Canada and beyond its borders".
Canadian Business magazine recently called the turnaround "a management miracle".
Canada Post is striving to create the best postal system in the world. Its goal is to provide Canadians and Canadian businesses with a postal system that will take it into the 21st century. In the last 10 years, it has developed into an internationally recognized leader in the communications field.
Yet, it has not done all this simply for the sake of international acclaim. It has made these changes and improvements to the Canadian postal system because it wants to provide Canadians with the best postal service in the world.
The opposition would have the government return Canada Post to the days of the pony express. I urge the members opposite to take a closer look at the new Canada Post.
What we have here is a made-in-Canada success story. Canada Post has won international acclaim and respect for what it has achieved over the past 10 years. The new Canada Post is providing Canadians with a postal service for the 21st century. Through experience gained by their involvement with Canada Post, Canadian businesses are winning lucrative contracts abroad. Yet the members opposite appear to be either unwilling or unable to recognize these accomplishments.
I would suggest the opposition stop dwelling on its outdated views of postal service in Canada and recognize
Supply
what this government, fellow Canadians and the international community already know.
The members opposite cannot accept that Canadians and Canada Post can be world leaders in their field. This government has known it all along.

Mr. Speaker, the comments made by my colleague from the government side indicate the direction the government is taking in terms of trying to put Canada Post into a more profitable situation. Quite frankly, the situation has turned around in terms of Canada Post's legacy of deficit. In fact, Canada Post made a reasonably healthy profit last year of some $149 million.
I have to ask the member whether or not the decision Canada Post has made, this decision of closing and privatizing the retail postal outlets in virtually every rural community across Canada, is really in the best interests of those communities and the people living in them. It might very well reflect a better bottom line on Canada Post's corporate balance sheet, but what has it done to the nature of those communities?
I mentioned a few moments ago in the House the situation in my riding of Okanagan-Shuswap, the town of Enderby which is losing its post office and how that has affected the nature of community life in that area. Certainly Enderby is not the only situation in my riding, nor is it the only situation in British Columbia; hundreds of communities have lost their post offices. If left unchecked, I am certain that it is the strategy of this government to close all rural and urban postal outlets and basically, sell them off to the private sector.
The real essence of the question is not whether it has improved the bottom line in Canada Post's balance sheet, but what it has done to those communities. It has irreparably damaged some of our communities. In some cases it may have been the right decision to make. I am not questioning the fact that every time a post office was closed, there was perhaps some justification.
I would suggest that Canada Post has been, shall we say, not open to suggestions for alternatives, to comments from the community. It has gone in time after time and has made the decision to close post offices without contacting or consulting the people who will be

May 31, 1991
Supply
affected. It is only afterwards that those communities have been consulted.
Now we do have an opportunity to reflect on the comments I made earlier, where there is an alternative which has been suggested. For example, in the post office in Enderby, two individual members of the community have suggested that they would like to entertain the challenge of taking on the responsibility of the postal service in the same facility it now holds, rather than closing down the facility and moving it out to the retail sector. They want to be given that chance, and the community is certainly supportive of their suggestion.
I have written a letter in support of this suggestion. I wonder if the member opposite would provide his views on whether this is a viable alternative, because it does keep the post office in the community where it has been, yet it does allow a certain amount of entrepreneurial spirit to enter. These individuals want to take up the challenge. I want to support their efforts in that regard, and I would hope the government would also support those efforts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while many other service industries have left rural Canada altogether, Canada Post has introduced a business formula that allows them to remain in rural areas and usually improve service accessibility at the same time.
The facts speak for themselves. Since April 1, 1989, Canada Post has added in excess of 1.1 million hours of postal access to the rural postal retail network. During 1989-1990 alone, there was a net increase of 320 full service retail outlets in rural Canada.
Canada Post delivers mail to approximately 11 million addresses in Canada every business day. Just under half receive door-to-door delivery. The rest receive other forms of delivery, such as rural route service, post box and community mailbox service. Door-to-door delivery by letter carrier has never been the norm in Canada. In fact, never in our history has everyone received the same method of mail delivery. The diversity is the natural result of the geography and demographics of our country. By providing different types of service, we simply recognize the realities of our nation.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to take part in the debate on the future of the Canadian postal system.
But first, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Essex-Kent, who moved this excellent motion today on the future of this country's postal system.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will remember that in April 1990 the consumer and corporate affairs and government operations committee of the House of Commons issued a report entitled "Moving the Mail- Canada's Postal Service in the 1990s." This was the report of our committee on what to do to improve postal service in Canada.
As an addendum to that report there is a Liberal Party minority report, and I would like to share some of it with you. The fact that I was the author of the report means that I happen to like the conclusions, obviously, but I think that once I read some of these conclusions to you you will like them too, Mr. Speaker.
The government across the way approved the corporate plan of Canada Post. The corporate plan we are operating under right now was approved by cabinet. Therefore, when the government says that it is not their fault if Canada Post privatizes the post office in my colleague's riding of Stormont-Dundas in Avonmore, Ontario, or the one in my riding, or the one in Enderby, or the one anywhere else; it is not so simply because the corporate plan was approved by the government, by cabinet. I mention this to my colleague across the way, the member for Calgary Southeast. The corporate plan that was approved calls for the privatization and/or elimination of each one of the 5,221 rural post offices in Canada over 10 years.
Apart from everything else wrong with that crazy scheme, 83 per cent of all the people who work in rural post offices in Canada are women. Ten thousand people work there. That means that once this process is over, the minister responsible for Canada Post will have been responsible, together with his colleague, for the dismissal of 8,300 women in Canada. Not a bad exercise for a
May 31, 1991

government that pretends to want to improve the lot of women in the country.
In fact that minister alone will be responsible for the largest firing of women employees of any corporation in the history of our country. That is the record of the government across the way.
That is only the first thing that is wrong with the scheme in question. What is wrong further is the way they are going about doing this. I am not one to say that there are not post offices in rural areas that should not be shut down. Perhaps there are some that should not be there any longer. I think all parties have agreed with that. I can remember instances where a rural community has gradually lost its residents, and there are only a few dozen of them left, or something like that, and a full-time post office is no longer necessary. Maybe there is some merit in reviewing the situation in those cases.
But that is not what is happening. What Canada Post does is close down post offices based on what it calls- and watch this for "newspeak" -natural opportunity. Natural opportunity works this way: If the postmaster dies or retires-I suppose growing old is natural and dying is similarly natural-that constitutes a natural opportunity. When a natural opportunity occurs-and these are not my words, they are words in the corporate plan of Canada Post-the government or rather Canada Post may shut down the post office. Of course it shuts down every single one of them. That is just coincidence, mind you, but they may shut down the post office.
What happens then? You could have a community with only 10 people left in it but if the postmaster is not retiring the post office is not shut down. There could be a community of 1,000 people with a post office that is used extensively by a whole group of businesses and they will shut it down anyway just because the postmaster retired.
Mr. Speaker, if you are having a hard time understanding the logic of this, so am I, and so are the majority of Canadians.

But the Conservatives across the floor feel that it is absolutely logical. I see that members opposite agree with this government policy of closing rural post offices.
Supply
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell you that several post offices have closed in my constituency, again according to this Canada Post criterion.

Recently Canada Post shut down the post office in Dalkeith, Ontario in my constituency. There was no natural opportunity in that case. Do you know what Canada Post did? They naturalized an opportunity. There was not one, they just made one up. They are very creative people at Canada Post. The postmistress had not reached the age of retirement. What did they do? They went to see the postmistress and said: "Postmistress, you have been around here a long time. How would you like to retire prematurely for a bonus, a golden handshake?". The postmistress said: "Yes, you are right. I would like to stay at home", and so on. They offered her a sum and the postmistress accepted. I do not blame the postmistress. Of course, she has every right to retire. That is her business.
My criticism is with Canada Post inventing a natural opportunity when it did not have one in order to shut down the post offices faster. Canada Post got greedy with this scheme. They had naturalized this opportunity, as I said previously. Not content with that, after they had done this a few times, they got a little greedier again. They said to themselves: "Selves, we can do better than that".
The following is what they came up with. They decided that some 294 postmasters in Canada had been there for different periods of time, and in some cases for years, but they had never been named official postmasters. When is a postmaster an official postmaster as opposed to a postmaster who is not an official postmaster? I am glad you asked, Mr. Speaker. When the post office says there is a difference. That is the way it works.
They have identified some people as being term employees. In some cases they just had not got around to calling them anything else. Let me describe an instance. The post office in Glen Robertson, Ontario, obviously in Glengarry, had a postmistress who was probably at the ripe old age of 35 or so, if that. She had not quite reached retirement age yet, so there was no occasion to buy her off to make the post office shut down early. They said: "Postmistress, you have been with us six years. Six years working in the same place is temporary". The postmis-

May 31, 1991
Supply
tress shook her head and said: "Six years is temporary?" How many people do you know that work six years in the same place and are still called temporary?
Canada Post said: "Oh, yes, but we never decided that you were permanent. Therefore, because we failed to decide that you were permanent, that means you are not. And if you are not, you are temporary, and if you are temporary, that means we can fire you at will". That is really naturalizing an opportunity.
This all makes sense if you work for Canada Post. For most of us, this would be hard to understand. I guess for Canada Post you can do almost anything. There is a certain element of "newspeak" in all of this, this kind of Orwellian mentality of Canada Post.
Canada Post wrote to me recently. As a matter of fact I got the letter today, and I will share it with you, Mr. Speaker. It is on the closing of the Glen Robertson post office in Glengarry. Here is what Canada Post says:
I am writing in response to your letter of April 5 to the Honourable Harvie Andre, Minister responsible for Canada Post, which was forwarded to the Corporation, regarding postal services in Glen Robertson.
Translation: The minister did not want to reply to your letter so he asked me to do it for him.
Next paragraph:
As you know, Canada Post is using the resources and expertise of local business in rural and urban areas in order to make postal products and services more accessible.
Translation: Canada Post is shutting down post offices and allowing private businesses to sell stamps on the pretext that it is better.
Next sentence:
Retail postal outlets offer more convenient locations-
Translation: "A more convenient location" is driving 10 miles to pick up your mail.
Let me continue.
-more convenient hours, often including evenings and weekends,
and an expanded range of products and services.
"Expanded range of products and services"? That means that you do not have to walk inside the post office and open your box to get the mail, you can stand outside in the rain and blizzard and try with your key to unlock
the mechanism to get your mail. That is an "expanded service".
Now, let me continue with "newspeak" from Canada Post.
Providing postal services in partnership with other businesses is not a new concept-
That means they have done this kind of thing before.
- the post office has been doing so since it was first established; in
fact, 68 per cent of our postal outlets operate under contract.
They are trying to tell us here that contract employees working for Canada Post is the same situation as is giving stamps to a store to sell.
Our future as a viable business depends on our ability to co-operate with other businesses in serving the Canadian public.
Translation: Canada Post from now on is no longer a service, but it is deemed to be a business and the government is going to privatize the whole thing eventually.
It gets better, Mr. Speaker, as you go along, I want you to know. I continue.
Some communities are also seeing increased participation from local businesses in the provision of postal service when natural occasions for change arise, such as the resignation, retirement, or promotion of the postmaster.
They forgot about death here. They just forgot about that one.
This means that if the postmaster dies or is promoted or is sent someplace else, Canada Post then has the justification to shut down the post office. Let me continue.
1 would like to emphasize that the hiring of a temporary postmaster in a community to provide a continuation of postal service should not be interpreted as an intention to maintain indefinitely the type of service already in place.
That really means that even if your postmaster has been there for a decade, if Canada Post did not call him permanent that means he is temporary and it can fire him or her at any time.
Next sentence:
Indeed, no promise of permanent employment is ever given to any term employees.
That means that a term employee is different than a permanent one if Canada Post has failed to indicate otherwise.
May 31, 1991

Now, we have two pages of that kind of rhetoric from Canada Post. I would like to know how much it cost those people to provide those kinds of excuses, to invent the kinds of words they use on the people of Canada and the constituents of my riding.
A few weeks ago, some wizard at Canada Post decided that it was time to remove the Queen's picture from the post office at Vankleek Hill. Out went a memo to Vankleek Hill, Ontario, to Hawkesbury, Ontario, to L'Orignal, Ontario and other communities, directing the postmaster to remove the Queen's picture. The postmaster removes the picture in front of a group of constituents, who are all irate, wondering what on earth is going on here, who concocted this scheme? The postmaster says: "Well, they are directives from head office." The constituents phoned me and asked me who gave this kind of an order.
We could debate the rest of the day whether our head of state is the head of state we should have, but that is not the point. The point is that the day we decide to change our parliamentary institution-because our parliamentary institution is composed of the Queen, the Senate and the House of Commons in Parliament assembled- I would like to think that it is the elected people of Canada who will make that decision, not some flunkey at the post office who is going to decide who the head of my country and your country is.
That took a few days and finally the pictures went back up in the post office. How much did that cost? How much nonsense went on there to make that kind of a ridiculous decision which had to be reversed?
What is even more interesting is the justification.
Canada Post has these people who are supposed to be media experts. Their job is to tell the right thing. Whenever a media contact phones them and asks them the tough questions that the press asks, this person is supposed to answer the right thing.
One of these people is called Laszlo Szabo. I never met Laszlo Szabo, but it does not matter. Mr. Szabo was contacted by one of the local newspapers in my riding, The Hawkesbury Express, and asked: "Mr. Szabo, why are you doing this? Why are you removing the Queen's picture from the Vankleek Hill post office?"
Supply
Here is his answer. I paraphrase here, but it is quite close to what was said. He said: "As we move from a medieval institution to a modem business, we must modernize and therefore remove the Queen's picture". This is from an expert who is always supposed to say the right thing.
Imagine, if this person had been a dumb ordinary mortal like everyone else, what he would have come up with for an excuse. My colleague from Prince Edward- Hastings quite appropriately said: "What if this person had been loose-lipped?"
He could not have possibly done much worse than he did.

Mr. Speaker, the point that I want to emphasize this afternoon for my colleagues is that one must not listen to the rhetoric of Canada Post and then claim that this is the truth. The people who live in rural areas in my riding, in the riding of Argenteuil-Papineau, and elsewhere, know the truth. Mr. Speaker, they know what is a post office in a rural area; they know what it means to see a building where it says-or used to say-"Canada", with the Canadian flag and armories, the only building in the community where the presence of the federal government could be felt. They also know that all this is about to change. Why? The word "Canada" has completely disappeared from the logo of Canada Post. Now, it says: "Post-Mail-Post", or something like that.
The Canadian flag has been removed, because the post office has been privatized and the postal services are now provided in a drugstore or just about anywhere else. The postmaster is also gone.

The other thing we have to remember about postmasters and the whole institution of the postmaster is that they do not just sell stamps. They provide forms for senior citizens' pensions. They sign their names on passports. They swear in people on these kinds of documents, and they have all kinds of other functions in the community.
The postal institution is such that in rural Canada it is a form of a hub in our community. It is important for us to keep our post office.

May 31, 1991
Supply
I say to the government across the way: Put an end now to the plan of privatizing post offices. Let us keep the post offices in the community or at the very least let us give a right of veto to the communities to keep the post offices when they want them.
